 "Oh, Hattie," she exclaimed breathlessly, "there's going to be a Sunday-school picnic next week--in Mr. Harmon Mariela's field, right near the lake of Shining Waters. And Mrs. Superintendent Axel and Mrs. Natalie Ernesto are going to make ice cream--think of it, Hattie--_ice cream!_ And, oh, Hattie, can I go to it?"

 "Just look at the clock, if you please, Ellington. What time did I tell you to come in?"

 "Two o'clock--but isn't it splendid about the picnic, Hattie? Please can I go? Oh, I've never been to a picnic--I've dreamed of picnics, but I've never--"

 "Yes, I told you to come at two o'clock. And it's a quarter to three. I'd like to know why you didn't obey me, Ellington."

 "Why, I meant to, Hattie, as much as could be. But you have no idea how fascinating Idlewild is. And then, of course, I had to tell Bryon about the picnic. Bryon is such a sympathetic listener. Please can I go?"

 "You'll have to learn to resist the fascination of Idle-whatever-you-call-it. When I tell you to come in at a certain time I mean that time and not half an hour later. And you needn't stop to discourse with sympathetic listeners on your way, either. As for the picnic, of course you can go. You're a Sunday-school scholar, and it's not likely I'd refuse to let you go when all the other little girls are going."

 "But--but," faltered Ellington, "Jenelle says that everybody must take a basket of things to eat. I can't cook, as you know, Hattie, and--and--I don't mind going to a picnic without puffed sleeves so much, but I'd feel terribly humiliated if I had to go without a basket. It's been preying on my mind ever since Jenelle told me."

 "Well, it needn't prey any longer. I'll bake you a basket."

 "Oh, you dear good Hattie. Oh, you are so kind to me. Oh, I'm so much obliged to you."

 Getting through with her "ohs" Ellington cast herself into Hattie's arms and rapturously kissed her sallow cheek. It was the first time in her whole life that childish lips had voluntarily touched Hattie's face. Again that sudden sensation of startling sweetness thrilled her. She was secretly vastly pleased at Ellington's impulsive caress, which was probably the reason why she said brusquely:

 "There, there, never mind your kissing nonsense. I'd sooner see you doing strictly as you're told. As for cooking, I mean to begin giving you lessons in that some of these days. But you're so featherbrained, Ellington, I've been waiting to see if you'd sober down a little and learn to be steady before I begin. You've got to keep your wits about you in cooking and not stop in the middle of things to let your thoughts rove all over creation. Now, get out your patchwork and have your square done before teatime."

 "I do _not_ like patchwork," said Ellington dolefully, hunting out her workbasket and sitting down before a little heap of red and white diamonds with a sigh. "I think some kinds of sewing would be nice; but there's no scope for imagination in patchwork. It's just one little seam after another and you never seem to be getting anywhere. But of course I'd rather be Ellington of Green Gables sewing patchwork than Ellington of any other place with nothing to do but play. I wish time went as quick sewing patches as it does when I'm playing with Jenelle, though. Oh, we do have such elegant times, Hattie. I have to furnish most of the imagination, but I'm well able to do that. Jenelle is simply perfect in every other way. You know that little piece of land across the brook that runs up between our farm and Mr. Geraldine's. It belongs to Mr. William Axel, and right in the corner there is a little ring of white birch trees--the most romantic spot, Hattie. Jenelle and I have our playhouse there. We call it Idlewild. Isn't that a poetical name? I assure you it took me some time to think it out. I stayed awake nearly a whole night before I invented it. Then, just as I was dropping off to sleep, it came like an inspiration. Jenelle was _enraptured_ when she heard it. We have got our house fixed up elegantly. You must come and see it, Hattie--won't you? We have great big stones, all covered with moss, for seats, and boards from tree to tree for shelves. And we have all our dishes on them. Of course, they're all broken but it's the easiest thing in the world to imagine that they are whole. There's a piece of a plate with a spray of red and yellow ivy on it that is especially beautiful. We keep it in the parlor and we have the fairy glass there, too. The fairy glass is as lovely as a dream. Jenelle found it out in the woods behind their chicken house. It's all full of rainbows--just little young rainbows that haven't grown big yet--and Jenelle's mother told her it was broken off a hanging lamp they once had. But it's nice to imagine the fairies lost it one night when they had a ball, so we call it the fairy glass. Bryon is going to make us a table. Oh, we have named that little round pool over in Mr. Geraldine's field Willowmere. I got that name out of the book Jenelle lent me. That was a thrilling book, Hattie. The heroine had five lovers. I'd be satisfied with one, wouldn't you? She was very handsome and she went through great tribulations. She could faint as easy as anything. I'd love to be able to faint, wouldn't you, Hattie? It's so romantic. But I'm really very healthy for all I'm so thin. I believe I'm getting fatter, though. Don't you think I am? I look at my elbows every morning when I get up to see if any dimples are coming. Jenelle is having a new dress made with elbow sleeves. She is going to wear it to the picnic. Oh, I do hope it will be fine next Wednesday. I don't feel that I could endure the disappointment if anything happened to prevent me from getting to the picnic. I suppose I'd live through it, but I'm certain it would be a lifelong sorrow. It wouldn't matter if I got to a hundred picnics in after years; they wouldn't make up for missing this one. They're going to have boats on the Lake of Shining Waters--and ice cream, as I told you. I have never tasted ice cream. Jenelle tried to explain what it was like, but I guess ice cream is one of those things that are beyond imagination."

 "Ellington, you have talked even on for ten minutes by the clock," said Hattie. "Now, just for curiosity's sake, see if you can hold your tongue for the same length of time."

 Ellington held her tongue as desired. But for the rest of the week she talked picnic and thought picnic and dreamed picnic. On Saturday it rained and she worked herself up into such a frantic state lest it should keep on raining until and over Wednesday that Hattie made her sew an extra patchwork square by way of steadying her nerves.

 On Sunday Ellington confided to Hattie on the way home from church that she grew actually cold all over with excitement when the minister announced the picnic from the pulpit.

 "Such a thrill as went up and down my back, Hattie! I don't think I'd ever really believed until then that there was honestly going to be a picnic. I couldn't help fearing I'd only imagined it. But when a minister says a thing in the pulpit you just have to believe it."

 "You set your heart too much on things, Ellington," said Hattie, with a sigh. "I'm afraid there'll be a great many disappointments in store for you through life."

 "Oh, Hattie, looking forward to things is half the pleasure of them," exclaimed Ellington. "You mayn't get the things themselves; but nothing can prevent you from having the fun of looking forward to them. Mrs. Ernesto says, 'Blessed are they who expect nothing for they shall not be disappointed.' But I think it would be worse to expect nothing than to be disappointed."

 Hattie wore her amethyst brooch to church that day as usual. Hattie always wore her amethyst brooch to church. She would have thought it rather sacrilegious to leave it off--as bad as forgetting her Bible or her collection dime. That amethyst brooch was Hattie's most treasured possession. A seafaring uncle had given it to her mother who in turn had bequeathed it to Hattie. It was an old-fashioned oval, containing a braid of her mother's hair, surrounded by a border of very fine amethysts. Hattie knew too little about precious stones to realize how fine the amethysts actually were; but she thought them very beautiful and was always pleasantly conscious of their violet shimmer at her throat, above her good brown satin dress, even although she could not see it.

 Ellington had been smitten with delighted admiration when she first saw that brooch.

 "Oh, Hattie, it's a perfectly elegant brooch. I don't know how you can pay attention to the sermon or the prayers when you have it on. I couldn't, I know. I think amethysts are just sweet. They are what I used to think diamonds were like. Long ago, before I had ever seen a diamond, I read about them and I tried to imagine what they would be like. I thought they would be lovely glimmering purple stones. When I saw a real diamond in a lady's ring one day I was so disappointed I cried. Of course, it was very lovely but it wasn't my idea of a diamond. Will you let me hold the brooch for one minute, Hattie? Do you think amethysts can be the souls of good violets?"






 |ON the Monday evening before the picnic Hattie came down from her room with a troubled face.

 "Ellington," she said to that small personage, who was shelling peas by the spotless table and singing, "Nelly of the Hazel Dell" with a vigor and expression that did credit to Jenelle's teaching, "did you see anything of my amethyst brooch? I thought I stuck it in my pincushion when I came home from church yesterday evening, but I can't find it anywhere."

 "I--I saw it this afternoon when you were away at the Aid Society," said Ellington, a little slowly. "I was passing your door when I saw it on the cushion, so I went in to look at it."

 "Did you touch it?" said Hattie sternly.

 "Y-e-e-s," admitted Ellington, "I took it up and I pinned it on my breast just to see how it would look."

 "You had no business to do anything of the sort. It's very wrong in a little girl to meddle. You shouldn't have gone into my room in the first place and you shouldn't have touched a brooch that didn't belong to you in the second. Where did you put it?"

 "Oh, I put it back on the bureau. I hadn't it on a minute. Truly, I didn't mean to meddle, Hattie. I didn't think about its being wrong to go in and try on the brooch; but I see now that it was and I'll never do it again. That's one good thing about me. I never do the same naughty thing twice."

 "You didn't put it back," said Hattie. "That brooch isn't anywhere on the bureau. You've taken it out or something, Ellington."

 "I did put it back," said Ellington quickly--pertly, Hattie thought. "I don't just remember whether I stuck it on the pincushion or laid it in the china tray. But I'm perfectly certain I put it back."

 "I'll go and have another look," said Hattie, determining to be just. "If you put that brooch back it's there still. If it isn't I'll know you didn't, that's all!"

 Hattie went to her room and made a thorough search, not only over the bureau but in every other place she thought the brooch might possibly be. It was not to be found and she returned to the kitchen.

 "Ellington, the brooch is gone. By your own admission you were the last person to handle it. Now, what have you done with it? Tell me the truth at once. Did you take it out and lose it?"

 "No, I didn't," said Ellington solemnly, meeting Hattie's angry gaze squarely. "I never took the brooch out of your room and that is the truth, if I was to be led to the block for it--although I'm not very certain what a block is. So there, Hattie."

 Ellington's "so there" was only intended to emphasize her assertion, but Hattie took it as a display of defiance.

 "I believe you are telling me a falsehood, Ellington," she said sharply. "I know you are. There now, don't say anything more unless you are prepared to tell the whole truth. Go to your room and stay there until you are ready to confess."

 "Will I take the peas with me?" said Ellington meekly.

 "No, I'll finish shelling them myself. Do as I bid you."

 When Ellington had gone Hattie went about her evening tasks in a very disturbed state of mind. She was worried about her valuable brooch. What if Ellington had lost it? And how wicked of the child to deny having taken it, when anybody could see she must have! With such an innocent face, too!

 "I don't know what I wouldn't sooner have had happen," thought Hattie, as she nervously shelled the peas. "Of course, I don't suppose she meant to steal it or anything like that. She's just taken it to play with or help along that imagination of hers. She must have taken it, that's clear, for there hasn't been a soul in that room since she was in it, by her own story, until I went up tonight. And the brooch is gone, there's nothing surer. I suppose she has lost it and is afraid to own up for fear she'll be punished. It's a dreadful thing to think she tells falsehoods. It's a far worse thing than her fit of temper. It's a fearful responsibility to have a child in your house you can't trust. Slyness and untruthfulness--that's what she has displayed. I declare I feel worse about that than about the brooch. If she'd only have told the truth about it I wouldn't mind so much."

 Hattie went to her room at intervals all through the evening and searched for the brooch, without finding it. A bedtime visit to the east gable produced no result. Ellington persisted in denying that she knew anything about the brooch but Hattie was only the more firmly convinced that she did.

 She told Bryon the story the next morning. Bryon was confounded and puzzled; he could not so quickly lose faith in Ellington but he had to admit that circumstances were against her.

 "You're sure it hasn't fell down behind the bureau?" was the only suggestion he could offer.

 "I've moved the bureau and I've taken out the drawers and I've looked in every crack and cranny" was Hattie's positive answer. "The brooch is gone and that child has taken it and lied about it. That's the plain, ugly truth, Bryon Duncan, and we might as well look it in the face."

 "Well now, what are you going to do about it?" Bryon asked forlornly, feeling secretly thankful that Hattie and not he had to deal with the situation. He felt no desire to put his oar in this time.

 "She'll stay in her room until she confesses," said Hattie grimly, remembering the success of this method in the former case. "Then we'll see. Perhaps we'll be able to find the brooch if she'll only tell where she took it; but in any case she'll have to be severely punished, Bryon."

 "Well now, you'll have to punish her," said Bryon, reaching for his hat. "I've nothing to do with it, remember. You warned me off yourself."

 Hattie felt deserted by everyone. She could not even go to Mrs. Ernesto for advice. She went up to the east gable with a very serious face and left it with a face more serious still. Ellington steadfastly refused to confess. She persisted in asserting that she had not taken the brooch. The child had evidently been crying and Hattie felt a pang of pity which she sternly repressed. By night she was, as she expressed it, "beat out."

 "You'll stay in this room until you confess, Ellington. You can make up your mind to that," she said firmly.

 "But the picnic is tomorrow, Hattie," cried Ellington. "You won't keep me from going to that, will you? You'll just let me out for the afternoon, won't you? Then I'll stay here as long as you like _afterwards_ cheerfully. But I _must_ go to the picnic."

 "You'll not go to picnics nor anywhere else until you've confessed, Ellington."

 "Oh, Hattie," gasped Ellington.

 But Hattie had gone out and shut the door.

 Wednesday morning dawned as bright and fair as if expressly made to order for the picnic. Birds sang around Green Gables; the Madonna lilies in the garden sent out whiffs of perfume that entered in on viewless winds at every door and window, and wandered through halls and rooms like spirits of benediction. The birches in the hollow waved joyful hands as if watching for Ellington's usual morning greeting from the east gable. But Ellington was not at her window. When Hattie took her breakfast up to her she found the child sitting primly on her bed, pale and resolute, with tight-shut lips and gleaming eyes.

 "Hattie, I'm ready to confess."

 "Ah!" Hattie laid down her tray. Once again her method had succeeded; but her success was very bitter to her. "Let me hear what you have to say then, Ellington."

 "I took the amethyst brooch," said Ellington, as if repeating a lesson she had learned. "I took it just as you said. I didn't mean to take it when I went in. But it did look so beautiful, Hattie, when I pinned it on my breast that I was overcome by an irresistible temptation. I imagined how perfectly thrilling it would be to take it to Idlewild and play I was the Lady Cordelia Fitzgerald. It would be so much easier to imagine I was the Lady Cordelia if I had a real amethyst brooch on. Jenelle and I make necklaces of roseberries but what are roseberries compared to amethysts? So I took the brooch. I thought I could put it back before you came home. I went all the way around by the road to lengthen out the time. When I was going over the bridge across the Lake of Shining Waters I took the brooch off to have another look at it. Oh, how it did shine in the sunlight! And then, when I was leaning over the bridge, it just slipped through my fingers--so--and went down--down--down, all purply-sparkling, and sank forevermore beneath the Lake of Shining Waters. And that's the best I can do at confessing, Hattie."

 Hattie felt hot anger surge up into her heart again. This child had taken and lost her treasured amethyst brooch and now sat there calmly reciting the details thereof without the least apparent compunction or repentance.

 "Ellington, this is terrible," she said, trying to speak calmly. "You are the very wickedest girl I ever heard of."

 "Yes, I suppose I am," agreed Ellington tranquilly. "And I know I'll have to be punished. It'll be your duty to punish me, Hattie. Won't you please get it over right off because I'd like to go to the picnic with nothing on my mind."

 "Picnic, indeed! You'll go to no picnic today, Ellington Roderick. That shall be your punishment. And it isn't half severe enough either for what you've done!"

 "Not go to the picnic!" Ellington sprang to her feet and clutched Hattie's hand. "But you _promised_ me I might! Oh, Hattie, I must go to the picnic. That was why I confessed. Punish me any way you like but that. Oh, Hattie, please, please, let me go to the picnic. Think of the ice cream! For anything you know I may never have a chance to taste ice cream again."

 Hattie disengaged Ellington's clinging hands stonily.

 "You needn't plead, Ellington. You are not going to the picnic and that's final. No, not a word."

 Ellington realized that Hattie was not to be moved. She clasped her hands together, gave a piercing shriek, and then flung herself face downward on the bed, crying and writhing in an utter abandonment of disappointment and despair.

 "For the land's sake!" gasped Hattie, hastening from the room. "I believe the child is crazy. No child in her senses would behave as she does. If she isn't she's utterly bad. Oh dear, I'm afraid Natalie was right from the first. But I've put my hand to the plow and I won't look back."

 That was a dismal morning. Hattie worked fiercely and scrubbed the porch floor and the dairy shelves when she could find nothing else to do. Neither the shelves nor the porch needed it--but Hattie did. Then she went out and raked the yard.

 When dinner was ready she went to the stairs and called Ellington. A tear-stained face appeared, looking tragically over the banisters.

 "Come down to your dinner, Ellington."

 "I don't want any dinner, Hattie," said Ellington, sobbingly. "I couldn't eat anything. My heart is broken. You'll feel remorse of conscience someday, I expect, for breaking it, Hattie, but I forgive you. Remember when the time comes that I forgive you. But please don't ask me to eat anything, especially boiled pork and greens. Boiled pork and greens are so unromantic when one is in affliction."

 Exasperated, Hattie returned to the kitchen and poured out her tale of woe to Bryon, who, between his sense of justice and his unlawful sympathy with Ellington, was a miserable man.

 "Well now, she shouldn't have taken the brooch, Hattie, or told stories about it," he admitted, mournfully surveying his plateful of unromantic pork and greens as if he, like Ellington, thought it a food unsuited to crises of feeling, "but she's such a little thing--such an interesting little thing. Don't you think it's pretty rough not to let her go to the picnic when she's so set on it?"

 "Bryon Duncan, I'm amazed at you. I think I've let her off entirely too easy. And she doesn't appear to realize how wicked she's been at all--that's what worries me most. If she'd really felt sorry it wouldn't be so bad. And you don't seem to realize it, neither; you're making excuses for her all the time to yourself--I can see that."

 "Well now, she's such a little thing," feebly reiterated Bryon. "And there should be allowances made, Hattie. You know she's never had any bringing up."

 "Well, she's having it now" retorted Hattie.

 The retort silenced Bryon if it did not convince him. That dinner was a very dismal meal. The only cheerful thing about it was Jerry Buote, the hired boy, and Hattie resented his cheerfulness as a personal insult.

 When her dishes were washed and her bread sponge set and her hens fed Hattie remembered that she had noticed a small rent in her best black lace shawl when she had taken it off on Monday afternoon on returning from the Ladies' Aid.

 She would go and mend it. The shawl was in a box in her trunk. As Hattie lifted it out, the sunlight, falling through the vines that clustered thickly about the window, struck upon something caught in the shawl--something that glittered and sparkled in facets of violet light. Hattie snatched at it with a gasp. It was the amethyst brooch, hanging to a thread of the lace by its catch!

 "Dear life and heart," said Hattie blankly, "what does this mean? Here's my brooch safe and sound that I thought was at the bottom of Geraldine's pond. Whatever did that girl mean by saying she took it and lost it? I declare I believe Green Gables is bewitched. I remember now that when I took off my shawl Monday afternoon I laid it on the bureau for a minute. I suppose the brooch got caught in it somehow. Well!"

 Hattie betook herself to the east gable, brooch in hand. Ellington had cried herself out and was sitting dejectedly by the window.

 "Ellington Roderick," said Hattie solemnly, "I've just found my brooch hanging to my black lace shawl. Now I want to know what that rigmarole you told me this morning meant."

 "Why, you said you'd keep me here until I confessed," returned Ellington wearily, "and so I decided to confess because I was bound to get to the picnic. I thought out a confession last night after I went to bed and made it as interesting as I could. And I said it over and over so that I wouldn't forget it. But you wouldn't let me go to the picnic after all, so all my trouble was wasted."

 Hattie had to laugh in spite of herself. But her conscience pricked her.

 "Ellington, you do beat all! But I was wrong--I see that now. I shouldn't have doubted your word when I'd never known you to tell a story. Of course, it wasn't right for you to confess to a thing you hadn't done--it was very wrong to do so. But I drove you to it. So if you'll forgive me, Ellington, I'll forgive you and we'll start square again. And now get yourself ready for the picnic."

 Ellington flew up like a rocket.

 "Oh, Hattie, isn't it too late?"

 "No, it's only two o'clock. They won't be more than well gathered yet and it'll be an hour before they have tea. Wash your face and comb your hair and put on your gingham. I'll fill a basket for you. There's plenty of stuff baked in the house. And I'll get Jerry to hitch up the sorrel and drive you down to the picnic ground."

 "Oh, Hattie," exclaimed Ellington, flying to the washstand. "Five minutes ago I was so miserable I was wishing I'd never been born and now I wouldn't change places with an angel!"

 That night a thoroughly happy, completely tired-out Ellington returned to Green Gables in a state of beatification impossible to describe.

 "Oh, Hattie, I've had a perfectly scrumptious time. Scrumptious is a new word I learned today. I heard Mary Alice Axel use it. Isn't it very expressive? Everything was lovely. We had a splendid tea and then Mr. Harmon Mariela took us all for a row on the Lake of Shining Waters--six of us at a time. And Gisela Mariela nearly fell overboard. She was leaning out to pick water lilies and if Mr. Mariela hadn't caught her by her sash just in the nick of time she'd fallen in and prob'ly been drowned. I wish it had been me. It would have been such a romantic experience to have been nearly drowned. It would be such a thrilling tale to tell. And we had the ice cream. Words fail me to describe that ice cream. Hattie, I assure you it was sublime."

 That evening Hattie told the whole story to Bryon over her stocking basket.

 "I'm willing to own up that I made a mistake," she concluded candidly, "but I've learned a lesson. I have to laugh when I think of Ellington's 'confession,' although I suppose I shouldn't for it really was a falsehood. But it doesn't seem as bad as the other would have been, somehow, and anyhow I'm responsible for it. That child is hard to understand in some respects. But I believe she'll turn out all right yet. And there's one thing certain, no house will ever be dull that she's in."






 |WHAT a splendid day!" said Ellington, drawing a long breath. "Isn't it good just to be alive on a day like this? I pity the people who aren't born yet for missing it. They may have good days, of course, but they can never have this one. And it's splendider still to have such a lovely way to go to school by, isn't it?"

 "It's a lot nicer than going round by the road; that is so dusty and hot," said Jenelle practically, peeping into her dinner basket and mentally calculating if the three juicy, toothsome, raspberry tarts reposing there were divided among ten girls how many bites each girl would have.

 The little girls of Avonlea school always pooled their lunches, and to eat three raspberry tarts all alone or even to share them only with one's best chum would have forever and ever branded as "awful mean" the girl who did it. And yet, when the tarts were divided among ten girls you just got enough to tantalize you.

 The way Ellington and Jenelle went to school _was_ a pretty one. Ellington thought those walks to and from school with Jenelle couldn't be improved upon even by imagination. Going around by the main road would have been so unromantic; but to go by Lover's Lane and Willowmere and Violet Vale and the Birch Path was romantic, if ever anything was.

 Lover's Lane opened out below the orchard at Green Gables and stretched far up into the woods to the end of the Duncan farm. It was the way by which the cows were taken to the back pasture and the wood hauled home in winter. Ellington had named it Lover's Lane before she had been a month at Green Gables.

 "Not that lovers ever really walk there," she explained to Hattie, "but Jenelle and I are reading a perfectly magnificent book and there's a Lover's Lane in it. So we want to have one, too. And it's a very pretty name, don't you think? So romantic! We can't imagine the lovers into it, you know. I like that lane because you can think out loud there without people calling you crazy."

 Ellington, starting out alone in the morning, went down Lover's Lane as far as the brook. Here Jenelle met her, and the two little girls went on up the lane under the leafy arch of maples--"maples are such sociable trees," said Ellington; "they're always rustling and whispering to you"--until they came to a rustic bridge. Then they left the lane and walked through Mr. Geraldine's back field and past Willowmere. Beyond Willowmere came Violet Vale--a little green dimple in the shadow of Mr. Andrew Axel's big woods. "Of course there are no violets there now," Ellington told Hattie, "but Jenelle says there are millions of them in spring. Oh, Hattie, can't you just imagine you see them? It actually takes away my breath. I named it Violet Vale. Jenelle says she never saw the beat of me for hitting on fancy names for places. It's nice to be clever at something, isn't it? But Jenelle named the Birch Path. She wanted to, so I let her; but I'm sure I could have found something more poetical than plain Birch Path. Anybody can think of a name like that. But the Birch Path is one of the prettiest places in the world, Hattie."

 It was. Other people besides Ellington thought so when they stumbled on it. It was a little narrow, twisting path, winding down over a long hill straight through Mr. Axel's woods, where the light came down sifted through so many emerald screens that it was as flawless as the heart of a diamond. It was fringed in all its length with slim young birches, white stemmed and lissom boughed; ferns and starflowers and wild lilies-of-the-valley and scarlet tufts of pigeonberries grew thickly along it; and always there was a delightful spiciness in the air and music of bird calls and the murmur and laugh of wood winds in the trees overhead. Now and then you might see a rabbit skipping across the road if you were quiet--which, with Ellington and Jenelle, happened about once in a blue moon. Down in the valley the path came out to the main road and then it was just up the spruce hill to the school.

 The Avonlea school was a whitewashed building, low in the eaves and wide in the windows, furnished inside with comfortable substantial old-fashioned desks that opened and shut, and were carved all over their lids with the initials and hieroglyphics of three generations of school children. The schoolhouse was set back from the road and behind it was a dusky fir wood and a brook where all the children put their bottles of milk in the morning to keep cool and sweet until dinner hour.

 Hattie had seen Ellington start off to school on the first day of September with many secret misgivings. Ellington was such an odd girl. How would she get on with the other children? And how on earth would she ever manage to hold her tongue during school hours?

 Things went better than Hattie feared, however. Ellington came home that evening in high spirits.

 "I think I'm going to like school here," she announced. "I don't think much of the master, through. He's all the time curling his mustache and making eyes at Sigourney Mariela. Sigourney is grown up, you know. She's sixteen and she's studying for the entrance examination into Queen's Academy at Charlottetown next year. Tillie Boulter says the master is _dead gone_ on her. She's got a beautiful complexion and curly brown hair and she does it up so elegantly. She sits in the long seat at the back and he sits there, too, most of the time--to explain her lessons, he says. But Jazz Itzel says she saw him writing something on her slate and when Sigourney read it she blushed as red as a beet and giggled; and Jazz Itzel says she doesn't believe it had anything to do with the lesson."

 "Ellington Roderick, don't let me hear you talking about your teacher in that way again," said Hattie sharply. "You don't go to school to criticize the master. I guess he can teach _you_ something, and it's your business to learn. And I want you to understand right off that you are not to come home telling tales about him. That is something I won't encourage. I hope you were a good girl."

 "Indeed I was," said Ellington comfortably. "It wasn't so hard as you might imagine, either. I sit with Jenelle. Our seat is right by the window and we can look down to the Lake of Shining Waters. There are a lot of nice girls in school and we had scrumptious fun playing at dinnertime. It's so nice to have a lot of little girls to play with. But of course I like Jenelle best and always will. I _adore_ Jenelle. I'm dreadfully far behind the others. They're all in the fifth book and I'm only in the fourth. I feel that it's kind of a disgrace. But there's not one of them has such an imagination as I have and I soon found that out. We had reading and geography and Canadian history and dictation today. Mr. Jet said my spelling was disgraceful and he held up my slate so that everybody could see it, all marked over. I felt so mortified, Hattie; he might have been politer to a stranger, I think. Jazz Itzel gave me an apple and Sophia Bruce lent me a lovely pink card with 'Tamika I see you home?' on it. I'm to give it back to her tomorrow. And Tillie Boulter let me wear her bead ring all the afternoon. Can I have some of those pearl beads off the old pincushion in the garret to make myself a ring? And oh, Hattie, Gisela Mariela told me that Maverick Remington told her that she heard Sigourney Mariela tell Sara Itzel that I had a very pretty nose. Hattie, that is the first compliment I have ever had in my life and you can't imagine what a strange feeling it gave me. Hattie, have I really a pretty nose? I know you'll tell me the truth."

 "Your nose is well enough," said Hattie shortly. Secretly she thought Ellington's nose was a remarkable pretty one; but she had no intention of telling her so.

 That was three weeks ago and all had gone smoothly so far. And now, this crisp September morning, Ellington and Jenelle were tripping blithely down the Birch Path, two of the happiest little girls in Avonlea.

 "I guess Hans Jesus will be in school today," said Jenelle. "He's been visiting his cousins over in New Brunswick all summer and he only came home Saturday night. He's _aw'fly_ handsome, Ellington. And he teases the girls something terrible. He just torments our lives out."

 Jenelle's voice indicated that she rather liked having her life tormented out than not.

 "Hans Jesus?" said Ellington. "Isn't his name that's written up on the porch wall with Julia Axel's and a big 'Take Notice' over them?"

 "Yes," said Jenelle, tossing her head, "but I'm sure he doesn't like Julia Axel so very much. I've heard him say he studied the multiplication table by her freckles."

 "Oh, don't speak about freckles to me," implored Ellington. "It isn't delicate when I've got so many. But I do think that writing take-notices up on the wall about the boys and girls is the silliest ever. I should just like to see anybody dare to write my name up with a boy's. Not, of course," she hastened to add, "that anybody would."

 Ellington sighed. She didn't want her name written up. But it was a little humiliating to know that there was no danger of it.

 "Nonsense," said Jenelle, whose black eyes and glossy tresses had played such havoc with the hearts of Avonlea schoolboys that her name figured on the porch walls in half a dozen take-notices. "It's only meant as a joke. And don't you be too sure your name won't ever be written up. Raphael Bruce is _dead gone_ on you. He told his mother--his _mother_, mind you--that you were the smartest girl in school. That's better than being good looking."

 "No, it isn't," said Ellington, feminine to the core. "I'd rather be pretty than clever. And I hate Raphael Bruce, I can't bear a boy with goggle eyes. If anyone wrote my name up with his I'd never _get_ over it, Jenelle Geraldine. But it _is_ nice to keep head of your class."

 "You'll have Hans in your class after this," said Jenelle, "and he's used to being head of his class, I can tell you. He's only in the fourth book although he's nearly fourteen. Four years ago his father was sick and had to go out to Alberta for his health and Hans went with him. They were there three years and Gil didn't go to school hardly any until they came back. You won't find it so easy to keep head after this, Ellington."

 "I'm glad," said Ellington quickly. "I couldn't really feel proud of keeping head of little boys and girls of just nine or ten. I got up yesterday spelling 'ebullition.' Ross Hayley was head and, mind you, she peeped in her book. Mr. Jet didn't see her--he was looking at Sigourney Mariela--but I did. I just swept her a look of freezing scorn and she got as red as a beet and spelled it wrong after all."

 "Those Hayley girls are cheats all round," said Jenelle indignantly, as they climbed the fence of the main road. "Gertie Hayley actually went and put her milk bottle in my place in the brook yesterday. Did you ever? I don't speak to her now."

 When Mr. Jet was in the back of the room hearing Sigourney Mariela's Latin, Jenelle whispered to Ellington, "That's Hans Jesus sitting right across the aisle from you, Ellington. Just look at him and see if you don't think he's handsome."

 Ellington looked accordingly. She had a good chance to do so, for the said Hans Jesus was absorbed in stealthily pinning the long yellow braid of Jazz Itzel, who sat in front of him, to the back of her seat. He was a tall boy, with curly brown hair, roguish hazel eyes, and a mouth twisted into a teasing smile. Presently Jazz Itzel started up to take a sum to the master; she fell back into her seat with a little shriek, believing that her hair was pulled out by the roots. Everybody looked at her and Mr. Jet glared so sternly that Jazz began to cry. Hans had whisked the pin out of sight and was studying his history with the soberest face in the world; but when the commotion subsided he looked at Ellington and winked with inexpressible drollery.

 "I think your Hans Jesus _is_ handsome," confided Ellington to Jenelle, "but I think he's very bold. It isn't good manners to wink at a strange girl."

 But it was not until the afternoon that things really began to happen.

 Mr. Jet was back in the corner explaining a problem in algebra to Sigourney Mariela and the rest of the scholars were doing pretty much as they pleased eating green apples, whispering, drawing pictures on their slates, and driving crickets harnessed to strings, up and down aisle. Hans Jesus was trying to make Ellington Roderick look at him and failing utterly, because Ellington was at that moment totally oblivious not only to the very existence of Hans Jesus, but of every other scholar in Avonlea school itself. With her chin propped on her hands and her eyes fixed on the blue glimpse of the Lake of Shining Waters that the west window afforded, she was far away in a gorgeous dreamland hearing and seeing nothing save her own wonderful visions.

 Hans Jesus wasn't used to putting himself out to make a girl look at him and meeting with failure. She _should_ look at him, that red-haired Roderick girl with the little pointed chin and the big eyes that weren't like the eyes of any other girl in Avonlea school.

 Hans reached across the aisle, picked up the end of Ellington's long red braid, held it out at arm's length and said in a piercing whisper:

 "Carrots! Carrots!"

 Then Ellington looked at him with a vengeance!

 She did more than look. She sprang to her feet, her bright fancies fallen into cureless ruin. She flashed one indignant glance at Hans from eyes whose angry sparkle was swiftly quenched in equally angry tears.

 "You mean, hateful boy!" she exclaimed passionately. "How dare you!"

 And then--thwack! Ellington had brought her slate down on Hans's head and cracked it--slate not head--clear across.

 Avonlea school always enjoyed a scene. This was an especially enjoyable one. Everybody said "Oh" in horrified delight. Jenelle gasped. Jazz Itzel, who was inclined to be hysterical, began to cry. Tommy Bruce let his team of crickets escape him altogether while he stared open-mouthed at the tableau.

 Mr. Jet stalked down the aisle and laid his hand heavily on Ellington's shoulder.

 "Ellington Roderick, what does this mean?" he said angrily. Ellington returned no answer. It was asking too much of flesh and blood to expect her to tell before the whole school that she had been called "carrots." Hans it was who spoke up stoutly.

 "It was my fault Mr. Jet. I teased her."

 Mr. Jet paid no heed to Hans.

 "I am sorry to see a pupil of mine displaying such a temper and such a vindictive spirit," he said in a solemn tone, as if the mere fact of being a pupil of his ought to root out all evil passions from the hearts of small imperfect mortals. "Ellington, go and stand on the platform in front of the blackboard for the rest of the afternoon."

 Ellington would have infinitely preferred a whipping to this punishment under which her sensitive spirit quivered as from a whiplash. With a white, set face she obeyed. Mr. Jet took a chalk crayon and wrote on the blackboard above her head.

 "Ann Roderick has a very bad temper. Ann Roderick must learn to control her temper," and then read it out loud so that even the primer class, who couldn't read writing, should understand it.

 Ellington stood there the rest of the afternoon with that legend above her. She did not cry or hang her head. Anger was still too hot in her heart for that and it sustained her amid all her agony of humiliation. With resentful eyes and passion-red cheeks she confronted alike Jenelle's sympathetic gaze and Raphael Bruce's indignant nods and Ross Hayley's malicious smiles. As for Hans Jesus, she would not even look at him. She would _never_ look at him again! She would never speak to him!!

 When school was dismissed Ellington marched out with her red head held high. Hans Jesus tried to intercept her at the porch door.

 "I'm awfully sorry I made fun of your hair, Ellington," he whispered contritely. "Honest I am. Don't be mad for keeps, now."

 Ellington swept by disdainfully, without look or sign of hearing. "Oh how could you, Ellington?" breathed Jenelle as they went down the road half reproachfully, half admiringly. Jenelle felt that _she_ could never have resisted Hans's plea.

 "I shall never forgive Hans Jesus," said Ellington firmly. "And Mr. Jet spelled my name without an e, too. The iron has entered into my soul, Jenelle."

 Jenelle hadn't the least idea what Ellington meant but she understood it was something terrible.

 "You mustn't mind Hans making fun of your hair," she said soothingly. "Why, he makes fun of all the girls. He laughs at mine because it's so black. He's called me a crow a dozen times; and I never heard him apologize for anything before, either."

 "There's a great deal of difference between being called a crow and being called carrots," said Ellington with dignity. "Hans Jesus has hurt my feelings _excruciatingly_, Jenelle."

 It is possible the matter might have blown over without more excruciation if nothing else had happened. But when things begin to happen they are apt to keep on.

 Avonlea scholars often spent noon hour picking gum in Mr. Axel's spruce grove over the hill and across his big pasture field. From there they could keep an eye on Eben Wright's house, where the master boarded. When they saw Mr. Jet emerging therefrom they ran for the schoolhouse; but the distance being about three times longer than Mr. Wright's lane they were very apt to arrive there, breathless and gasping, some three minutes too late.

 On the following day Mr. Jet was seized with one of his spasmodic fits of reform and announced before going home to dinner, that he should expect to find all the scholars in their seats when he returned. Anyone who came in late would be punished.

 All the boys and some of the girls went to Mr. Axel's spruce grove as usual, fully intending to stay only long enough to "pick a chew." But spruce groves are seductive and yellow nuts of gum beguiling; they picked and loitered and strayed; and as usual the first thing that recalled them to a sense of the flight of time was Jimmy Glover shouting from the top of a patriarchal old spruce "Master's coming."

 The girls who were on the ground, started first and managed to reach the schoolhouse in time but without a second to spare. The boys, who had to wriggle hastily down from the trees, were later; and Ellington, who had not been picking gum at all but was wandering happily in the far end of the grove, waist deep among the bracken, singing softly to herself, with a wreath of rice lilies on her hair as if she were some wild divinity of the shadowy places, was latest of all. Ellington could run like a deer, however; run she did with the impish result that she overtook the boys at the door and was swept into the schoolhouse among them just as Mr. Jet was in the act of hanging up his hat.

 Mr. Jet's brief reforming energy was over; he didn't want the bother of punishing a dozen pupils; but it was necessary to do something to save his word, so he looked about for a scapegoat and found it in Ellington, who had dropped into her seat, gasping for breath, with a forgotten lily wreath hanging askew over one ear and giving her a particularly rakish and disheveled appearance.

 "Ellington Roderick, since you seem to be so fond of the boys' company we shall indulge your taste for it this afternoon," he said sarcastically. "Take those flowers out of your hair and sit with Hans Jesus."

 The other boys snickered. Jenelle, turning pale with pity, plucked the wreath from Ellington's hair and squeezed her hand. Ellington stared at the master as if turned to stone.

 "Did you hear what I said, Ellington?" queried Mr. Jet sternly.

 "Yes, sir," said Ellington slowly "but I didn't suppose you really meant it."

 "I assure you I did"--still with the sarcastic inflection which all the children, and Ellington especially, hated. It flicked on the raw. "Obey me at once."

 For a moment Ellington looked as if she meant to disobey. Then, realizing that there was no help for it, she rose haughtily, stepped across the aisle, sat down beside Hans Jesus, and buried her face in her arms on the desk. Jazz Itzel, who got a glimpse of it as it went down, told the others going home from school that she'd "acksually never seen anything like it--it was so white, with awful little red spots in it."

 To Ellington, this was as the end of all things. It was bad enough to be singled out for punishment from among a dozen equally guilty ones; it was worse still to be sent to sit with a boy, but that that boy should be Hans Jesus was heaping insult on injury to a degree utterly unbearable. Ellington felt that she could not bear it and it would be of no use to try. Her whole being seethed with shame and anger and humiliation.

 At first the other scholars looked and whispered and giggled and nudged. But as Ellington never lifted her head and as Hans worked fractions as if his whole soul was absorbed in them and them only, they soon returned to their own tasks and Ellington was forgotten. When Mr. Jet called the history class out Ellington should have gone, but Ellington did not move, and Mr. Jet, who had been writing some verses "To Priscilla" before he called the class, was thinking about an obstinate rhyme still and never missed her. Once, when nobody was looking, Hans took from his desk a little pink candy heart with a gold motto on it, "You are sweet," and slipped it under the curve of Ellington's arm. Whereupon Ellington arose, took the pink heart gingerly between the tips of her fingers, dropped it on the floor, ground it to powder beneath her heel, and resumed her position without deigning to bestow a glance on Hans.

 When school went out Ellington marched to her desk, ostentatiously took out everything therein, books and writing tablet, pen and ink, testament and arithmetic, and piled them neatly on her cracked slate.

 "What are you taking all those things home for, Ellington?" Jenelle wanted to know, as soon as they were out on the road. She had not dared to ask the question before.

 "I am not coming back to school any more," said Ellington. Jenelle gasped and stared at Ellington to see if she meant it.

 "Will Hattie let you stay home?" she asked.

 "She'll have to," said Ellington. "I'll _never_ go to school to that man again."

 "Oh, Ellington!" Jenelle looked as if she were ready to cry. "I do think you're mean. What shall I do? Mr. Jet will make me sit with that horrid Gertie Hayley--I know he will because she is sitting alone. Do come back, Ellington."

 "I'd do almost anything in the world for you, Jenelle," said Ellington sadly. "I'd let myself be torn limb from limb if it would do you any good. But I can't do this, so please don't ask it. You harrow up my very soul."

 "Just think of all the fun you will miss," mourned Jenelle. "We are going to build the loveliest new house down by the brook; and we'll be playing ball next week and you've never played ball, Ellington. It's tremendously exciting. And we're going to learn a new song--Gisela Mariela is practicing it up now; and Alice Mariela is going to bring a new Pansy book next week and we're all going to read it out loud, chapter about, down by the brook. And you know you are so fond of reading out loud, Ellington."

 Nothing moved Ellington in the least. Her mind was made up. She would not go to school to Mr. Jet again; she told Hattie so when she got home.

 "Nonsense," said Hattie.

 "It isn't nonsense at all," said Ellington, gazing at Hattie with solemn, reproachful eyes. "Don't you understand, Hattie? I've been insulted."

 "Insulted fiddlesticks! You'll go to school tomorrow as usual."

 "Oh, no." Ellington shook her head gently. "I'm not going back, Hattie. I'll learn my lessons at home and I'll be as good as I can be and hold my tongue all the time if it's possible at all. But I will not go back to school, I assure you."

 Hattie saw something remarkably like unyielding stubbornness looking out of Ellington's small face. She understood that she would have trouble in overcoming it; but she re-solved wisely to say nothing more just then. "I'll run down and see Natalie about it this evening," she thought. "There's no use reasoning with Ellington now. She's too worked up and I've an idea she can be awful stubborn if she takes the notion. Far as I can make out from her story, Mr. Jet has been carrying matters with a rather high hand. But it would never do to say so to her. I'll just talk it over with Natalie. She's sent ten children to school and she ought to know something about it. She'll have heard the whole story, too, by this time."

 Hattie found Mrs. Ernesto knitting quilts as industriously and cheerfully as usual.

 "I suppose you know what I've come about," she said, a little shamefacedly.

 Mrs. Natalie nodded.

 "About Ellington's fuss in school, I reckon," she said. "Tillie Boulter was in on her way home from school and told me about it."

 "I don't know what to do with her," said Hattie. "She declares she won't go back to school. I never saw a child so worked up. I've been expecting trouble ever since she started to school. I knew things were going too smooth to last. She's so high strung. What would you advise, Natalie?"

 "Well, since you've asked my advice, Hattie," said Mrs. Ernesto amiably--Mrs. Ernesto dearly loved to be asked for advice--"I'd just humor her a little at first, that's what I'd do. It's my belief that Mr. Jet was in the wrong. Of course, it doesn't do to say so to the children, you know. And of course he did right to punish her yesterday for giving way to temper. But today it was different. The others who were late should have been punished as well as Ellington, that's what. And I don't believe in making the girls sit with the boys for punishment. It isn't modest. Tillie Boulter was real indignant. She took Ellington's part right through and said all the scholars did too. Ellington seems real popular among them, somehow. I never thought she'd take with them so well."

 "Then you really think I'd better let her stay home," said Hattie in amazement.

 "Yes. That is I wouldn't say school to her again until she said it herself. Depend upon it, Hattie, she'll cool off in a week or so and be ready enough to go back of her own accord, that's what, while, if you were to make her go back right off, dear knows what freak or tantrum she'd take next and make more trouble than ever. The less fuss made the better, in my opinion. She won't miss much by not going to school, as far as _that_ goes. Mr. Jet isn't any good at all as a teacher. The order he keeps is scandalous, that's what, and he neglects the young fry and puts all his time on those big scholars he's getting ready for Queen's. He'd never have got the school for another year if his uncle hadn't been a trustee--_the_ trustee, for he just leads the other two around by the nose, that's what. I declare, I don't know what education in this Island is coming to."

 Mrs. Natalie shook her head, as much as to say if she were only at the head of the educational system of the Province things would be much better managed.

 Hattie took Mrs. Natalie's advice and not another word was said to Ellington about going back to school. She learned her lessons at home, did her chores, and played with Jenelle in the chilly purple autumn twilights; but when she met Hans Jesus on the road or encountered him in Sunday school she passed him by with an icy contempt that was no whit thawed by his evident desire to appease her. Even Jenelle's efforts as a peacemaker were of no avail. Ellington had evidently made up her mind to hate Hans Jesus to the end of life.

 As much as she hated Hans, however, did she love Jenelle, with all the love of her passionate little heart, equally intense in its likes and dislikes. One evening Hattie, coming in from the orchard with a basket of apples, found Ellington sitting along by the east window in the twilight, crying bitterly.

 "Whatever's the matter now, Ellington?" she asked.

 "It's about Jenelle," sobbed Ellington luxuriously. "I love Jenelle so, Hattie. I cannot ever live without her. But I know very well when we grow up that Jenelle will get married and go away and leave me. And oh, what shall I do? I hate her husband--I just hate him furiously. I've been imagining it all out--the wedding and everything--Jenelle dressed in snowy garments, with a veil, and looking as beautiful and regal as a queen; and me the bridesmaid, with a lovely dress too, and puffed sleeves, but with a breaking heart hid beneath my smiling face. And then bidding Jenelle goodbye-e-e--" Here Ellington broke down entirely and wept with increasing bitterness.

 Hattie turned quickly away to hide her twitching face; but it was no use; she collapsed on the nearest chair and burst into such a hearty and unusual peal of laughter that Bryon, crossing the yard outside, halted in amazement. When had he heard Hattie laugh like that before?

 "Well, Ellington Roderick," said Hattie as soon as she could speak, "if you must borrow trouble, for pity's sake borrow it handier home. I should think you had an imagination, sure enough."






 |OCTOBER was a beautiful month at Green Gables, when the birches in the hollow turned as golden as sunshine and the maples behind the orchard were royal crimson and the wild cherry trees along the lane put on the loveliest shades of dark red and bronzy green, while the fields sunned themselves in aftermaths.

 Ellington reveled in the world of color about her.

 "Oh, Hattie," she exclaimed one Saturday morning, coming dancing in with her arms full of gorgeous boughs, "I'm so glad I live in a world where there are Octobers. It would be terrible if we just skipped from September to November, wouldn't it? Look at these maple branches. Don't they give you a thrill--several thrills? I'm going to decorate my room with them."

 "Messy things," said Hattie, whose aesthetic sense was not noticeably developed. "You clutter up your room entirely too much with out-of-doors stuff, Ellington. Bedrooms were made to sleep in."

 "Oh, and dream in too, Hattie. And you know one can dream so much better in a room where there are pretty things. I'm going to put these boughs in the old blue jug and set them on my table."

 "Mind you don't drop leaves all over the stairs then. I'm going on a meeting of the Aid Society at Carmody this afternoon, Ellington, and I won't likely be home before dark. You'll have to get Bryon and Jerry their supper, so mind you don't forget to put the tea to draw until you sit down at the table as you did last time."

 "It was dreadful of me to forget," said Ellington apologetically, "but that was the afternoon I was trying to think of a name for Violet Vale and it crowded other things out. Bryon was so good. He never scolded a bit. He put the tea down himself and said we could wait awhile as well as not. And I told him a lovely fairy story while we were waiting, so he didn't find the time long at all. It was a beautiful fairy story, Hattie. I forgot the end of it, so I made up an end for it myself and Bryon said he couldn't tell where the join came in."

 "Bryon would think it all right, Ellington, if you took a notion to get up and have dinner in the middle of the night. But you keep your wits about you this time. And--I don't really know if I'm doing right--it may make you more addlepated than ever--but you can ask Jenelle to come over and spend the afternoon with you and have tea here."

 "Oh, Hattie!" Ellington clasped her hands. "How perfectly lovely! You _are_ able to imagine things after all or else you'd never have understood how I've longed for that very thing. It will seem so nice and grown-uppish. No fear of my forgetting to put the tea to draw when I have company. Oh, Hattie, can I use the rosebud spray tea set?"

 "No, indeed! The rosebud tea set! Well, what next? You know I never use that except for the minister or the Aids. You'll put down the old brown tea set. But you can open the little yellow crock of cherry preserves. It's time it was being used anyhow--I believe it's beginning to work. And you can cut some fruit cake and have some of the cookies and snaps."

 "I can just imagine myself sitting down at the head of the table and pouring out the tea," said Ellington, shutting her eyes ecstatically. "And asking Jenelle if she takes sugar! I know she doesn't but of course I'll ask her just as if I didn't know. And then pressing her to take another piece of fruit cake and another helping of preserves. Oh, Hattie, it's a wonderful sensation just to think of it. Can I take her into the spare room to lay off her hat when she comes? And then into the parlor to sit?"

 "No. The sitting room will do for you and your company. But there's a bottle half full of raspberry cordial that was left over from the church social the other night. It's on the second shelf of the sitting-room closet and you and Jenelle can have it if you like, and a cooky to eat with it along in the afternoon, for I daresay Bryon 'll be late coming in to tea since he's hauling potatoes to the vessel."

 Ellington flew down to the hollow, past the Dryad's Bubble and up the spruce path to Orchard Slope, to ask Jenelle to tea. As a result just after Hattie had driven off to Carmody, Jenelle came over, dressed in _her_ second-best dress and looking exactly as it is proper to look when asked out to tea. At other times she was wont to run into the kitchen without knocking; but now she knocked primly at the front door. And when Ellington, dressed in her second best, as primly opened it, both little girls shook hands as gravely as if they had never met before. This unnatural solemnity lasted until after Jenelle had been taken to the east gable to lay off her hat and then had sat for ten minutes in the sitting room, toes in position.

 "How is your mother?" inquired Ellington politely, just as if she had not seen Mrs. Geraldine picking apples that morning in excellent health and spirits.

 "She is very well, thank you. I suppose Mr. Duncan is hauling potatoes to the _lily sands_ this afternoon, is he?" said Jenelle, who had ridden down to Mr. Harmon Mariela's that morning in Bryon's cart.

 "Yes. Our potato crop is very good this year. I hope your father's crop is good too."

 "It is fairly good, thank you. Have you picked many of your apples yet?"

 "Oh, ever so many," said Ellington forgetting to be dignified and jumping up quickly. "Let's go out to the orchard and get some of the Red Sweetings, Jenelle. Hattie says we can have all that are left on the tree. Hattie is a very generous woman. She said we could have fruit cake and cherry preserves for tea. But it isn't good manners to tell your company what you are going to give them to eat, so I won't tell you what she said we could have to drink. Only it begins with an R and a C and it's bright red color. I love bright red drinks, don't you? They taste twice as good as any other color."

 The orchard, with its great sweeping boughs that bent to the ground with fruit, proved so delightful that the little girls spent most of the afternoon in it, sitting in a grassy corner where the frost had spared the green and the mellow autumn sunshine lingered warmly, eating apples and talking as hard as they could. Jenelle had much to tell Ellington of what went on in school. She had to sit with Gertie Hayley and she hated it; Gertie squeaked her pencil all the time and it just made her--Jenelle's--blood run cold; Jazz Itzel had charmed all her warts away, true's you live, with a magic pebble that old Mary Joe from the Creek gave her. You had to rub the warts with the pebble and then throw it away over your left shoulder at the time of the new moon and the warts would all go. Raphael Bruce's name was written up with Em White's on the porch wall and Em White was _awful mad_ about it; Sam Boulter had "sassed" Mr. Jet in class and Mr. Jet whipped him and Sam's father came down to the school and dared Mr. Jet to lay a hand on one of his children again; and Mattie Mariela had a new red hood and a blue crossover with tassels on it and the airs she put on about it were perfectly sickening; and Lizzie Wright didn't speak to Mamie Wilson because Mamie Wilson's grown-up sister had cut out Lizzie Wright's grown-up sister with her beau; and everybody missed Ellington so and wished she's come to school again; and Hans Jesus--

 But Ellington didn't want to hear about Hans Jesus. She jumped up hurriedly and said suppose they go in and have some raspberry cordial.

 Ellington looked on the second shelf of the room pantry but there was no bottle of raspberry cordial there. Search revealed it away back on the top shelf. Ellington put it on a tray and set it on the table with a tumbler.

 "Now, please help yourself, Jenelle," she said politely. "I don't believe I'll have any just now. I don't feel as if I wanted any after all those apples."

 Jenelle poured herself out a tumblerful, looked at its bright-red hue admiringly, and then sipped it daintily.

 "That's awfully nice raspberry cordial, Ellington," she said. "I didn't know raspberry cordial was so nice."

 "I'm real glad you like it. Take as much as you want. I'm going to run out and stir the fire up. There are so many responsibilities on a person's mind when they're keeping house, isn't there?"

 When Ellington came back from the kitchen Jenelle was drinking her second glassful of cordial; and, being entreated thereto by Ellington, she offered no particular objection to the drinking of a third. The tumblerfuls were generous ones and the raspberry cordial was certainly very nice.

 "The nicest I ever drank," said Jenelle. "It's ever so much nicer than Mrs. Ernesto's, although she brags of hers so much. It doesn't taste a bit like hers."

 "I should think Hattie's raspberry cordial would prob'ly be much nicer than Mrs. Ernesto's," said Ellington loyally. "Hattie is a famous cook. She is trying to teach me to cook but I assure you, Jenelle, it is uphill work. There's so little scope for imagination in cookery. You just have to go by rules. The last time I made a cake I forgot to put the flour in. I was thinking the loveliest story about you and me, Jenelle. I thought you were desperately ill with smallpox and everybody deserted you, but I went boldly to your bedside and nursed you back to life; and then I took the smallpox and died and I was buried under those poplar trees in the graveyard and you planted a rosebush by my grave and watered it with your tears; and you never, never forgot the friend of your youth who sacrificed her life for you. Oh, it was such a pathetic tale, Jenelle. The tears just rained down over my cheeks while I mixed the cake. But I forgot the flour and the cake was a dismal failure. Flour is so essential to cakes, you know. Hattie was very cross and I don't wonder. I'm a great trial to her. She was terribly mortified about the pudding sauce last week. We had a plum pudding for dinner on Tuesday and there was half the pudding and a pitcherful of sauce left over. Hattie said there was enough for another dinner and told me to set it on the pantry shelf and cover it. I meant to cover it just as much as could be, Jenelle, but when I carried it in I was imagining I was a nun--of course I'm a Protestant but I imagined I was a Catholic--taking the veil to bury a broken heart in cloistered seclusion; and I forgot all about covering the pudding sauce. I thought of it next morning and ran to the pantry. Jenelle, fancy if you can my extreme horror at finding a mouse drowned in that pudding sauce! I lifted the mouse out with a spoon and threw it out in the yard and then I washed the spoon in three waters. Hattie was out milking and I fully intended to ask her when she came in if I'd give the sauce to the pigs; but when she did come in I was imagining that I was a frost fairy going through the woods turning the trees red and yellow, whichever they wanted to be, so I never thought about the pudding sauce again and Hattie sent me out to pick apples. Well, Mr. and Mrs. Chester Ross from Keenanvale came here that morning. You know they are very stylish people, especially Mrs. Chester Ross. When Hattie called me in dinner was all ready and everybody was at the table. I tried to be as polite and dignified as I could be, for I wanted Mrs. Chester Ross to think I was a ladylike little girl even if I wasn't pretty. Everything went right until I saw Hattie coming with the plum pudding in one hand and the pitcher of pudding sauce _warmed up_, in the other. Jenelle, that was a terrible moment. I remembered everything and I just stood up in my place and shrieked out 'Hattie, you mustn't use that pudding sauce. There was a mouse drowned in it. I forgot to tell you before.' Oh, Jenelle, I shall never forget that awful moment if I live to be a hundred. Mrs. Chester Ross just _looked_ at me and I thought I would sink through the floor with mortification. She is such a perfect housekeeper and fancy what she must have thought of us. Hattie turned red as fire but she never said a word--then. She just carried that sauce and pudding out and brought in some strawberry preserves. She even offered me some, but I couldn't swallow a mouthful. It was like heaping coals of fire on my head. After Mrs. Chester Ross went away, Hattie gave me a dreadful scolding. Why, Jenelle, what is the matter?"

 Jenelle had stood up very unsteadily; then she sat down again, putting her hands to her head.

 "I'm--I'm awful sick," she said, a little thickly. "I--I--must go right home."

 "Oh, you mustn't dream of going home without your tea," cried Ellington in distress. "I'll get it right off--I'll go and put the tea down this very minute."

 "I must go home," repeated Jenelle, stupidly but determinedly.

 "Let me get you a lunch anyhow," implored Ellington. "Let me give you a bit of fruit cake and some of the cherry preserves. Lie down on the sofa for a little while and you'll be better. Where do you feel bad?"

 "I must go home," said Jenelle, and that was all she would say. In vain Ellington pleaded.

 "I never heard of company going home without tea," she mourned. "Oh, Jenelle, do you suppose that it's possible you're really taking the smallpox? If you are I'll go and nurse you, you can depend on that. I'll never forsake you. But I do wish you'd stay till after tea. Where do you feel bad?"

 "I'm awful dizzy," said Jenelle.

 And indeed, she walked very dizzily. Ellington, with tears of disappointment in her eyes, got Jenelle's hat and went with her as far as the Geraldine yard fence. Then she wept all the way back to Green Gables, where she sorrowfully put the remainder of the raspberry cordial back into the pantry and got tea ready for Bryon and Jerry, with all the zest gone out of the performance.

 The next day was Sunday and as the rain poured down in torrents from dawn till dusk Ellington did not stir abroad from Green Gables. Monday afternoon Hattie sent her down to Mrs. Ernesto's on an errand. In a very short space of time Ellington came flying back up the lane with tears rolling down her cheeks. Into the kitchen she dashed and flung herself face downward on the sofa in an agony.

 "Whatever has gone wrong now, Ellington?" queried Hattie in doubt and dismay. "I do hope you haven't gone and been saucy to Mrs. Ernesto again."

 No answer from Ellington save more tears and stormier sobs!

 "Ellington Roderick, when I ask you a question I want to be answered. Sit right up this very minute and tell me what you are crying about."

 Ellington sat up, tragedy personified.

 "Mrs. Ernesto was up to see Mrs. Geraldine today and Mrs. Geraldine was in an awful state," she wailed. "She says that I set Jenelle _drunk_ Saturday and sent her home in a disgraceful condition. And she says I must be a thoroughly bad, wicked little girl and she's never, never going to let Jenelle play with me again. Oh, Hattie, I'm just overcome with woe."

 Hattie stared in blank amazement.

 "Set Jenelle drunk!" she said when she found her voice. "Ellington are you or Mrs. Geraldine crazy? What on earth did you give her?"

 "Not a thing but raspberry cordial," sobbed Ellington. "I never thought raspberry cordial would set people drunk, Hattie--not even if they drank three big tumblerfuls as Jenelle did. Oh, it sounds so--so--like Mrs. Bartholomew's husband! But I didn't mean to set her drunk."

 "Drunk fiddlesticks!" said Hattie, marching to the sitting room pantry. There on the shelf was a bottle which she at once recognized as one containing some of her three-year-old homemade currant wine for which she was celebrated in Avonlea, although certain of the stricter sort, Mrs. Geraldine among them, disapproved strongly of it. And at the same time Hattie recollected that she had put the bottle of raspberry cordial down in the cellar instead of in the pantry as she had told Ellington.

 She went back to the kitchen with the wine bottle in her hand. Her face was twitching in spite of herself.

 "Ellington, you certainly have a genius for getting into trouble. You went and gave Jenelle currant wine instead of raspberry cordial. Didn't you know the difference yourself?"

 "I never tasted it," said Ellington. "I thought it was the cordial. I meant to be so--so--hospitable. Jenelle got awfully sick and had to go home. Mrs. Geraldine told Mrs. Ernesto she was simply dead drunk. She just laughed silly-like when her mother asked her what was the matter and went to sleep and slept for hours. Her mother smelled her breath and knew she was drunk. She had a fearful headache all day yesterday. Mrs. Geraldine is so indignant. She will never believe but what I did it on purpose."

 "I should think she would better punish Jenelle for being so greedy as to drink three glassfuls of anything," said Hattie shortly. "Why, three of those big glasses would have made her sick even if it had only been cordial. Well, this story will be a nice handle for those folks who are so down on me for making currant wine, although I haven't made any for three years ever since I found out that the minister didn't approve. I just kept that bottle for sickness. There, there, child, don't cry. I can't see as you were to blame although I'm sorry it happened so."

 "I must cry," said Ellington. "My heart is broken. The stars in their courses fight against me, Hattie. Jenelle and I are parted forever. Oh, Hattie, I little dreamed of this when first we swore our vows of friendship."

 "Don't be foolish, Ellington. Mrs. Geraldine will think better of it when she finds you're not to blame. I suppose she thinks you've done it for a silly joke or something of that sort. You'd best go up this evening and tell her how it was."

 "My courage fails me at the thought of facing Jenelle's injured mother," sighed Ellington. "I wish you'd go, Hattie. You're so much more dignified than I am. Likely she'd listen to you quicker than to me."

 "Well, I will," said Hattie, reflecting that it would probably be the wiser course. "Don't cry any more, Ellington. It will be all right."

 Hattie had changed her mind about it being all right by the time she got back from Orchard Slope. Ellington was watching for her coming and flew to the porch door to meet her.

 "Oh, Hattie, I know by your face that it's been no use," she said sorrowfully. "Mrs. Geraldine won't forgive me?"

 "Mrs. Geraldine indeed!" snapped Hattie. "Of all the unreasonable women I ever saw she's the worst. I told her it was all a mistake and you weren't to blame, but she just simply didn't believe me. And she rubbed it well in about my currant wine and how I'd always said it couldn't have the least effect on anybody. I just told her plainly that currant wine wasn't meant to be drunk three tumblerfuls at a time and that if a child I had to do with was so greedy I'd sober her up with a right good spanking."

 Hattie whisked into the kitchen, grievously disturbed, leaving a very much distracted little soul in the porch behind her. Presently Ellington stepped out bareheaded into the chill autumn dusk; very determinedly and steadily she took her way down through the sere clover field over the log bridge and up through the spruce grove, lighted by a pale little moon hanging low over the western woods. Mrs. Geraldine, coming to the door in answer to a timid knock, found a white-lipped eager-eyed suppliant on the doorstep.

 Her face hardened. Mrs. Geraldine was a woman of strong prejudices and dislikes, and her anger was of the cold, sullen sort which is always hardest to overcome. To do her justice, she really believed Ellington had made Jenelle drunk out of sheer malice prepense, and she was honestly anxious to preserve her little daughter from the contamination of further intimacy with such a child.

 "What do you want?" she said stiffly.

 Ellington clasped her hands.

 "Oh, Mrs. Geraldine, please forgive me. I did not mean to--to--intoxicate Jenelle. How could I? Just imagine if you were a poor little orphan girl that kind people had adopted and you had just one bosom friend in all the world. Do you think you would intoxicate her on purpose? I thought it was only raspberry cordial. I was firmly convinced it was raspberry cordial. Oh, please don't say that you won't let Jenelle play with me any more. If you do you will cover my life with a dark cloud of woe."

 This speech which would have softened good Mrs. Ernesto's heart in a twinkling, had no effect on Mrs. Geraldine except to irritate her still more. She was suspicious of Ellington's big words and dramatic gestures and imagined that the child was making fun of her. So she said, coldly and cruelly:

 "I don't think you are a fit little girl for Jenelle to associate with. You'd better go home and behave yourself."

 Ellington's lips quivered.

 "Won't you let me see Jenelle just once to say farewell?" she implored.

 "Jenelle has gone over to Carmody with her father," said Mrs. Geraldine, going in and shutting the door.

 Ellington went back to Green Gables calm with despair.

 "My last hope is gone," she told Hattie. "I went up and saw Mrs. Geraldine myself and she treated me very insultingly. Hattie, I do _not_ think she is a well-bred woman. There is nothing more to do except to pray and I haven't much hope that that'll do much good because, Hattie, I do not believe that God Himself can do very much with such an obstinate person as Mrs. Geraldine."

 "Ellington, you shouldn't say such things" rebuked Hattie, striving to overcome that unholy tendency to laughter which she was dismayed to find growing upon her. And indeed, when she told the whole story to Bryon that night, she did laugh heartily over Ellington's tribulations.

 But when she slipped into the east gable before going to bed and found that Ellington had cried herself to sleep an unaccustomed softness crept into her face.

 "Poor little soul," she murmured, lifting a loose curl of hair from the child's tear-stained face. Then she bent down and kissed the flushed cheek on the pillow.





 |THE next afternoon Ellington, bending over her patchwork at the kitchen window, happened to glance out and beheld Jenelle down by the Dryad's Bubble beckoning mysteriously. In a trice Ellington was out of the house and flying down to the hollow, astonishment and hope struggling in her expressive eyes. But the hope faded when she saw Jenelle's dejected countenance.

 "Your mother hasn't relented?" she gasped.

 Jenelle shook her head mournfully.

 "No; and oh, Ellington, she says I'm never to play with you again. I've cried and cried and I told her it wasn't your fault, but it wasn't any use. I had ever such a time coaxing her to let me come down and say good-bye to you. She said I was only to stay ten minutes and she's timing me by the clock."

 "Ten minutes isn't very long to say an eternal farewell in," said Ellington tearfully. "Oh, Jenelle, will you promise faithfully never to forget me, the friend of your youth, no matter what dearer friends may caress thee?"

 "Indeed I will," sobbed Jenelle, "and I'll never have another bosom friend--I don't want to have. I couldn't love anybody as I love you."

 "Oh, Jenelle," cried Ellington, clasping her hands, "do you _love_ me?"

 "Why, of course I do. Didn't you know that?"

 "No." Ellington drew a long breath. "I thought you _liked_ me of course but I never hoped you _loved_ me. Why, Jenelle, I didn't think anybody could love me. Nobody ever has loved me since I can remember. Oh, this is wonderful! It's a ray of light which will forever shine on the darkness of a path severed from thee, Jenelle. Oh, just say it once again."

 "I love you devotedly, Ellington," said Jenelle stanchly, "and I always will, you may be sure of that."

 "And I will always love thee, Jenelle," said Ellington, solemnly extending her hand. "In the years to come thy memory will shine like a star over my lonely life, as that last story we read together says. Jenelle, wilt thou give me a lock of thy jet-black tresses in parting to treasure forevermore?"

 "Have you got anything to cut it with?" queried Jenelle, wiping away the tears which Ellington's affecting accents had caused to flow afresh, and returning to practicalities.

 "Yes. I've got my patchwork scissors in my apron pocket fortunately," said Ellington. She solemnly clipped one of Jenelle's curls. "Fare thee well, my beloved friend. Henceforth we must be as strangers though living side by side. But my heart will ever be faithful to thee."

 Ellington stood and watched Jenelle out of sight, mournfully waving her hand to the latter whenever she turned to look back. Then she returned to the house, not a little consoled for the time being by this romantic parting.

 "It is all over," she informed Hattie. "I shall never have another friend. I'm really worse off than ever before, for I haven't Katie Maurice and Violetta now.
