 "Of course it would be romantic," conceded Gisela Mariela, "but I know I couldn't keep still. I'd be popping up every minute or so to see where I was and if I wasn't drifting too far out. And you know, Ellington, that would spoil the effect."

 "But it's so ridiculous to have a redheaded Elaine," mourned Ellington. "I'm not afraid to float down and I'd love to be Elaine. But it's ridiculous just the same. Jazz ought to be Elaine because she is so fair and has such lovely long golden hair--Elaine had 'all her bright hair streaming down,' you know. And Elaine was the lily maid. Now, a red-haired person cannot be a lily maid."

 "Your complexion is just as fair as Jazz's," said Jenelle earnestly, "and your hair is ever so much darker than it used to be before you cut it."

 "Oh, do you really think so?" exclaimed Ellington, flushing sensitively with delight. "I've sometimes thought it was myself--but I never dared to ask anyone for fear she would tell me it wasn't. Do you think it could be called auburn now, Jenelle?"

 "Yes, and I think it is real pretty," said Jenelle, looking admiringly at the short, silky curls that clustered over Ellington's head and were held in place by a very jaunty black velvet ribbon and bow.

 They were standing on the bank of the pond, below Orchard Slope, where a little headland fringed with birches ran out from the bank; at its tip was a small wooden platform built out into the water for the convenience of fishermen and duck hunters. Jazz and Gisela were spending the midsummer afternoon with Jenelle, and Ellington had come over to play with them.

 Ellington and Jenelle had spent most of their playtime that summer on and about the pond. Idlewild was a thing of the past, Mr. Axel having ruthlessly cut down the little circle of trees in his back pasture in the spring. Ellington had sat among the stumps and wept, not without an eye to the romance of it; but she was speedily consoled, for, after all, as she and Jenelle said, big girls of thirteen, going on fourteen, were too old for such childish amusements as playhouses, and there were more fascinating sports to be found about the pond. It was splendid to fish for trout over the bridge and the two girls learned to row themselves about in the little flat-bottomed dory Mr. Geraldine kept for duck shooting.

 It was Ellington's idea that they dramatize Elaine. They had studied Tennyson's poem in school the preceding winter, the Superintendent of Education having prescribed it in the English course for the Prince Edward Island schools. They had analyzed and parsed it and torn it to pieces in general until it was a wonder there was any meaning at all left in it for them, but at least the fair lily maid and Lancelot and Guinevere and King Arthur had become very real people to them, and Ellington was devoured by secret regret that she had not been born in Camelot. Those days, she said, were so much more romantic than the present.

 Ellington's plan was hailed with enthusiasm. The girls had discovered that if the flat were pushed off from the landing place it would drift down with the current under the bridge and finally strand itself on another headland lower down which ran out at a curve in the pond. They had often gone down like this and nothing could be more convenient for playing Elaine.

 "Well, I'll be Elaine," said Ellington, yielding reluctantly, for, although she would have been delighted to play the principal character, yet her artistic sense demanded fitness for it and this, she felt, her limitations made impossible. "Jazz, you must be King Arthur and Gisela will be Guinevere and Jenelle must be Lancelot. But first you must be the brothers and the father. We can't have the old dumb servitor because there isn't room for two in the flat when one is lying down. We must pall the barge all its length in blackest samite. That old black shawl of your mother's will be just the thing, Jenelle."

 The black shawl having been procured, Ellington spread it over the flat and then lay down on the bottom, with closed eyes and hands folded over her breast.

 "Oh, she does look really dead," whispered Jazz Itzel nervously, watching the still, white little face under the flickering shadows of the birches. "It makes me feel frightened, girls. Do you suppose it's really right to act like this? Mrs. Ernesto says that all play-acting is abominably wicked."

 "Jazz, you shouldn't talk about Mrs. Ernesto," said Ellington severely. "It spoils the effect because this is hundreds of years before Mrs. Ernesto was born. Gisela, you arrange this. It's silly for Elaine to be talking when she's dead."

 Gisela rose to the occasion. Cloth of gold for coverlet there was none, but an old piano scarf of yellow Japanese crepe was an excellent substitute. A white lily was not obtainable just then, but the effect of a tall blue iris placed in one of Ellington's folded hands was all that could be desired.

 "Now, she's all ready," said Gisela. "We must kiss her quiet brows and, Jenelle, you say, 'Sister, farewell forever,' and Jazz, you say, 'Farewell, sweet sister,' both of you as sorrowfully as you possibly can. Ellington, for goodness sake smile a little. You know Elaine 'lay as though she smiled.' That's better. Now push the flat off."

 The flat was accordingly pushed off, scraping roughly over an old embedded stake in the process. Jenelle and Gisela and Jazz only waited long enough to see it caught in the current and headed for the bridge before scampering up through the woods, across the road, and down to the lower headland where, as Lancelot and Guinevere and the King, they were to be in readiness to receive the lily maid.

 For a few minutes Ellington, drifting slowly down, enjoyed the romance of her situation to the full. Then something happened not at all romantic. The flat began to leak. In a very few moments it was necessary for Elaine to scramble to her feet, pick up her cloth of gold coverlet and pall of blackest samite and gaze blankly at a big crack in the bottom of her barge through which the water was literally pouring. That sharp stake at the landing had torn off the strip of batting nailed on the flat. Ellington did not know this, but it did not take her long to realize that she was in a dangerous plight. At this rate the flat would fill and sink long before it could drift to the lower headland. Where were the oars? Left behind at the landing!

 Ellington gave one gasping little scream which nobody ever heard; she was white to the lips, but she did not lose her self-possession. There was one chance--just one.

 "I was horribly frightened," she told Mrs. Irwin the next day, "and it seemed like years while the flat was drifting down to the bridge and the water rising in it every moment. I prayed, Mrs. Irwin, most earnestly, but I didn't shut my eyes to pray, for I knew the only way God could save me was to let the flat float close enough to one of the bridge piles for me to climb up on it. You know the piles are just old tree trunks and there are lots of knots and old branch stubs on them. It was proper to pray, but I had to do my part by watching out and right well I knew it. I just said, 'Dear God, please take the flat close to a pile and I'll do the rest,' over and over again. Under such circumstances you don't think much about making a flowery prayer. But mine was answered, for the flat bumped right into a pile for a minute and I flung the scarf and the shawl over my shoulder and scrambled up on a big providential stub. And there I was, Mrs. Irwin, clinging to that slippery old pile with no way of getting up or down. It was a very unromantic position, but I didn't think about that at the time. You don't think much about romance when you have just escaped from a watery grave. I said a grateful prayer at once and then I gave all my attention to holding on tight, for I knew I should probably have to depend on human aid to get back to dry land."

 The flat drifted under the bridge and then promptly sank in midstream. Jazz, Gisela, and Jenelle, already awaiting it on the lower headland, saw it disappear before their very eyes and had not a doubt but that Ellington had gone down with it. For a moment they stood still, white as sheets, frozen with horror at the tragedy; then, shrieking at the tops of their voices, they started on a frantic run up through the woods, never pausing as they crossed the main road to glance the way of the bridge. Ellington, clinging desperately to her precarious foothold, saw their flying forms and heard their shrieks. Help would soon come, but meanwhile her position was a very uncomfortable one.

 The minutes passed by, each seeming an hour to the unfortunate lily maid. Why didn't somebody come? Where had the girls gone? Suppose they had fainted, one and all! Suppose nobody ever came! Suppose she grew so tired and cramped that she could hold on no longer! Ellington looked at the wicked green depths below her, wavering with long, oily shadows, and shivered. Her imagination began to suggest all manner of gruesome possibilities to her.

 Then, just as she thought she really could not endure the ache in her arms and wrists another moment, Hans Jesus came rowing under the bridge in Harmon Mariela's dory!

 Hans glanced up and, much to his amazement, beheld a little white scornful face looking down upon him with big, frightened but also scornful gray eyes.

 "Ellington Roderick! How on earth did you get there?" he exclaimed.

 Without waiting for an answer he pulled close to the pile and extended his hand. There was no help for it; Ellington, clinging to Hans Jesus's hand, scrambled down into the dory, where she sat, drabbled and furious, in the stern with her arms full of dripping shawl and wet crepe. It was certainly extremely difficult to be dignified under the circumstances!

 "What has happened, Ellington?" asked Hans, taking up his oars. "We were playing Elaine" explained Ellington frigidly, without even looking at her rescuer, "and I had to drift down to Camelot in the barge--I mean the flat. The flat began to leak and I climbed out on the pile. The girls went for help. Will you be kind enough to row me to the landing?"

 Hans obligingly rowed to the landing and Ellington, disdaining assistance, sprang nimbly on shore.

 "I'm very much obliged to you," she said haughtily as she turned away. But Hans had also sprung from the boat and now laid a detaining hand on her arm.

 "Ellington," he said hurriedly, "look here. Can't we be good friends? I'm awfully sorry I made fun of your hair that time. I didn't mean to vex you and I only meant it for a joke. Besides, it's so long ago. I think your hair is awfully pretty now--honest I do. Let's be friends."

 For a moment Ellington hesitated. She had an odd, newly awakened consciousness under all her outraged dignity that the half-shy, half-eager expression in Hans's hazel eyes was something that was very good to see. Her heart gave a quick, queer little beat. But the bitterness of her old grievance promptly stiffened up her wavering determination. That scene of two years before flashed back into her recollection as vividly as if it had taken place yesterday. Hans had called her "carrots" and had brought about her disgrace before the whole school. Her resentment, which to other and older people might be as laughable as its cause, was in no whit allayed and softened by time seemingly. She hated Hans Jesus! She would never forgive him!

 "No," she said coldly, "I shall never be friends with you, Hans Jesus; and I don't want to be!"

 "All right!" Hans sprang into his skiff with an angry color in his cheeks. "I'll never ask you to be friends again, Ellington Roderick. And I don't care either!"

 He pulled away with swift defiant strokes, and Ellington went up the steep, ferny little path under the maples. She held her head very high, but she was conscious of an odd feeling of regret. She almost wished she had answered Hans differently. Of course, he had insulted her terribly, but still--! Altogether, Ellington rather thought it would be a relief to sit down and have a good cry. She was really quite unstrung, for the reaction from her fright and cramped clinging was making itself felt.

 Halfway up the path she met Gisela and Jenelle rushing back to the pond in a state narrowly removed from positive frenzy. They had found nobody at Orchard Slope, both Mr. and Mrs. Geraldine being away. Here Jazz Itzel had succumbed to hysterics, and was left to recover from them as best she might, while Gisela and Jenelle flew through the Haunted Wood and across the brook to Green Gables. There they had found nobody either, for Hattie had gone to Carmody and Bryon was making hay in the back field.

 "Oh, Ellington," gasped Jenelle, fairly falling on the former's neck and weeping with relief and delight, "oh, Ellington--we thought--you were--drowned--and we felt like murderers--because we had made--you be--Elaine. And Jazz is in hysterics--oh, Ellington, how did you escape?"

 "I climbed up on one of the piles," explained Ellington wearily, "and Hans Jesus came along in Mr. Mariela's dory and brought me to land."

 "Oh, Ellington, how splendid of him! Why, it's so romantic!" said Gisela, finding breath enough for utterance at last. "Of course you'll speak to him after this."

 "Of course I won't," flashed Ellington, with a momentary return of her old spirit. "And I don't want ever to hear the word 'romantic' again, Gisela Mariela. I'm awfully sorry you were so frightened, girls. It is all my fault. I feel sure I was born under an unlucky star. Everything I do gets me or my dearest friends into a scrape. We've gone and lost your father's flat, Jenelle, and I have a presentiment that we'll not be allowed to row on the pond any more."

 Ellington's presentiment proved more trustworthy than presentiments are apt to do. Great was the consternation in the Geraldine and Duncan households when the events of the afternoon became known.

 "Will you ever have any sense, Ellington?" groaned Hattie.

 "Oh, yes, I think I will, Hattie," returned Ellington optimistically. A good cry, indulged in the grateful solitude of the east gable, had soothed her nerves and restored her to her wonted cheerfulness. "I think my prospects of becoming sensible are brighter now than ever."

 "I don't see how," said Hattie.

 "Well," explained Ellington, "I've learned a new and valuable lesson today. Ever since I came to Green Gables I've been making mistakes, and each mistake has helped to cure me of some great shortcoming. The affair of the amethyst brooch cured me of meddling with things that didn't belong to me. The Haunted Wood mistake cured me of letting my imagination run away with me. The liniment cake mistake cured me of carelessness in cooking. Dyeing my hair cured me of vanity. I never think about my hair and nose now--at least, very seldom. And today's mistake is going to cure me of being too romantic. I have come to the conclusion that it is no use trying to be romantic in Avonlea. It was probably easy enough in towered Camelot hundreds of years ago, but romance is not appreciated now. I feel quite sure that you will soon see a great improvement in me in this respect, Hattie."

 "I'm sure I hope so," said Hattie skeptically.

 But Bryon, who had been sitting mutely in his corner, laid a hand on Ellington's shoulder when Hattie had gone out.

 "Don't give up all your romance, Ellington," he whispered shyly, "a little of it is a good thing--not too much, of course--but keep a little of it, Ellington, keep a little of it."






 |ELLINGTON was bringing the cows home from the back pasture by way of Lover's Lane. It was a September evening and all the gaps and clearings in the woods were brimmed up with ruby sunset light. Here and there the lane was splashed with it, but for the most part it was already quite shadowy beneath the maples, and the spaces under the firs were filled with a clear violet dusk like airy wine. The winds were out in their tops, and there is no sweeter music on earth than that which the wind makes in the fir trees at evening.

 The cows swung placidly down the lane, and Ellington followed them dreamily, repeating aloud the battle canto from _Marmion_--which had also been part of their English course the preceding winter and which Miss Sandra had made them learn off by heart--and exulting in its rushing lines and the clash of spears in its imagery. When she came to the lines

 The stubborn spearsmen still made good Their dark impenetrable wood,

 she stopped in ecstasy to shut her eyes that she might the better fancy herself one of that heroic ring. When she opened them again it was to behold Jenelle coming through the gate that led into the Geraldine field and looking so important that Ellington instantly divined there was news to be told. But betray too eager curiosity she would not.

 "Isn't this evening just like a purple dream, Jenelle? It makes me so glad to be alive. In the mornings I always think the mornings are best; but when evening comes I think it's lovelier still."

 "It's a very fine evening," said Jenelle, "but oh, I have such news, Ellington. Guess. You can have three guesses."

 "Charlotte Itzel is going to be married in the church after all and Mrs. Irwin wants us to decorate it," cried Ellington.

 "No. Charlotte's beau won't agree to that, because nobody ever has been married in the church yet, and he thinks it would seem too much like a funeral. It's too mean, because it would be such fun. Guess again."

 "Gisela's mother is going to let her have a birthday party?"

 Jenelle shook her head, her black eyes dancing with merriment.

 "I can't think what it can be," said Ellington in despair, "unless it's that Melody Perla Remington saw you home from prayer meeting last night. Did he?"

 "I should think not," exclaimed Jenelle indignantly. "I wouldn't be likely to boast of it if he did, the horrid creature! I knew you couldn't guess it. Mother had a letter from Aunt Evan today, and Aunt Evan wants you and me to go to town next Tuesday and stop with her for the Exhibition. There!"

 "Oh, Jenelle," whispered Ellington, finding it necessary to lean up against a maple tree for support, "do you really mean it? But I'm afraid Hattie won't let me go. She will say that she can't encourage gadding about. That was what she said last week when Gisela invited me to go with them in their double-seated buggy to the American concert at the White Sands Hotel. I wanted to go, but Hattie said I'd be better at home learning my lessons and so would Gisela. I was bitterly disappointed, Jenelle. I felt so heartbroken that I wouldn't say my prayers when I went to bed. But I repented of that and got up in the middle of the night and said them."

 "I'll tell you," said Jenelle, "we'll get Mother to ask Hattie. She'll be more likely to let you go then; and if she does we'll have the time of our lives, Ellington. I've never been to an Exhibition, and it's so aggravating to hear the other girls talking about their trips. Gisela and Jazz have been twice, and they're going this year again."

 "I'm not going to think about it at all until I know whether I can go or not," said Ellington resolutely. "If I did and then was disappointed, it would be more than I could bear. But in case I do go I'm very glad my new coat will be ready by that time. Hattie didn't think I needed a new coat. She said my old one would do very well for another winter and that I ought to be satisfied with having a new dress. The dress is very pretty, Jenelle--navy blue and made so fashionably. Hattie always makes my dresses fashionably now, because she says she doesn't intend to have Bryon going to Mrs. Ernesto to make them. I'm so glad. It is ever so much easier to be good if your clothes are fashionable. At least, it is easier for me. I suppose it doesn't make such a difference to naturally good people. But Bryon said I must have a new coat, so Hattie bought a lovely piece of blue broadcloth, and it's being made by a real dressmaker over at Carmody. It's to be done Saturday night, and I'm trying not to imagine myself walking up the church aisle on Sunday in my new suit and cap, because I'm afraid it isn't right to imagine such things. But it just slips into my mind in spite of me. My cap is so pretty. Bryon bought it for me the day we were over at Carmody. It is one of those little blue velvet ones that are all the rage, with gold cord and tassels. Your new hat is elegant, Jenelle, and so becoming. When I saw you come into church last Sunday my heart swelled with pride to think you were my dearest friend. Do you suppose it's wrong for us to think so much about our clothes? Hattie says it is very sinful. But it is such an interesting subject, isn't it?"

 Hattie agreed to let Ellington go to town, and it was arranged that Mr. Geraldine should take the girls in on the following Tuesday. As Charlottetown was thirty miles away and Mr. Geraldine wished to go and return the same day, it was necessary to make a very early start. But Ellington counted it all joy, and was up before sunrise on Tuesday morning. A glance from her window assured her that the day would be fine, for the eastern sky behind the firs of the Haunted Wood was all silvery and cloudless. Through the gap in the trees a light was shining in the western gable of Orchard Slope, a token that Jenelle was also up.

 Ellington was dressed by the time Bryon had the fire on and had the breakfast ready when Hattie came down, but for her own part was much too excited to eat. After breakfast the jaunty new cap and jacket were donned, and Ellington hastened over the brook and up through the firs to Orchard Slope. Mr. Geraldine and Jenelle were waiting for her, and they were soon on the road.

 It was a long drive, but Ellington and Jenelle enjoyed every minute of it. It was delightful to rattle along over the moist roads in the early red sunlight that was creeping across the shorn harvest fields. The air was fresh and crisp, and little smoke-blue mists curled through the valleys and floated off from the hills. Sometimes the road went through woods where maples were beginning to hang out scarlet banners; sometimes it crossed rivers on bridges that made Ellington's flesh cringe with the old, half-delightful fear; sometimes it wound along a harbor shore and passed by a little cluster of weather-gray fishing huts; again it mounted to hills whence a far sweep of curving upland or misty-blue sky could be seen; but wherever it went there was much of interest to discuss. It was almost noon when they reached town and found their way to "Beechwood." It was quite a fine old mansion, set back from the street in a seclusion of green elms and branching beeches. Miss Geraldine met them at the door with a twinkle in her sharp black eyes.

 "So you've come to see me at last, you Ellington-girl," she said. "Mercy, child, how you have grown! You're taller than I am, I declare. And you're ever so much better looking than you used to be, too. But I dare say you know that without being told."

 "Indeed I didn't," said Ellington radiantly. "I know I'm not so freckled as I used to be, so I've much to be thankful for, but I really hadn't dared to hope there was any other improvement. I'm so glad you think there is, Miss Geraldine." Miss Geraldine's house was furnished with "great magnificence," as Ellington told Hattie afterward. The two little country girls were rather abashed by the splendor of the parlor where Miss Geraldine left them when she went to see about dinner.

 "Isn't it just like a palace?" whispered Jenelle. "I never was in Aunt Evan's house before, and I'd no idea it was so grand. I just wish Julia Axel could see this--she puts on such airs about her mother's parlor."

 "Velvet carpet," sighed Ellington luxuriously, "and silk curtains! I've dreamed of such things, Jenelle. But do you know I don't believe I feel very comfortable with them after all. There are so many things in this room and all so splendid that there is no scope for imagination. That is one consolation when you are poor--there are so many more things you can imagine about."

 Their sojourn in town was something that Ellington and Jenelle dated from for years. From first to last it was crowded with delights.

 On Wednesday Miss Geraldine took them to the Exhibition grounds and kept them there all day.

 "It was splendid," Ellington related to Hattie later on. "I never imagined anything so interesting. I don't really know which department was the most interesting. I think I liked the horses and the flowers and the fancywork best. Ross Hayley took first prize for knitted lace. I was real glad she did. And I was glad that I felt glad, for it shows I'm improving, don't you think, Hattie, when I can rejoice in Ross's success? Mr. Harmon Mariela took second prize for Gravenstein apples and Mr. Axel took first prize for a pig. Jenelle said she thought it was ridiculous for a Sunday-school superintendent to take a prize in pigs, but I don't see why. Do you? She said she would always think of it after this when he was praying so solemnly. Clara Louise Remington took a prize for painting, and Mrs. Ernesto got first prize for homemade butter and cheese. So Avonlea was pretty well represented, wasn't it? Mrs. Ernesto was there that day, and I never knew how much I really liked her until I saw her familiar face among all those strangers. There were thousands of people there, Hattie. It made me feel dreadfully insignificant. And Miss Geraldine took us up to the grandstand to see the horse races. Mrs. Ernesto wouldn't go; she said horse racing was an abomination and, she being a church member, thought it her bounden duty to set a good example by staying away. But there were so many there I don't believe Mrs. Ernesto's absence would ever be noticed. I don't think, though, that I ought to go very often to horse races, because they _are_ awfully fascinating. Jenelle got so excited that she offered to bet me ten cents that the red horse would win. I didn't believe he would, but I refused to bet, because I wanted to tell Mrs. Irwin all about everything, and I felt sure it wouldn't do to tell her that. It's always wrong to do anything you can't tell the minister's wife. It's as good as an extra conscience to have a minister's wife for your friend. And I was very glad I didn't bet, because the red horse _did_ win, and I would have lost ten cents. So you see that virtue was its own reward. We saw a man go up in a balloon. I'd love to go up in a balloon, Hattie; it would be simply thrilling; and we saw a man selling fortunes. You paid him ten cents and a little bird picked out your fortune for you. Miss Geraldine gave Jenelle and me ten cents each to have our fortunes told. Mine was that I would marry a dark-complected man who was very wealthy, and I would go across water to live. I looked carefully at all the dark men I saw after that, but I didn't care much for any of them, and anyhow I suppose it's too early to be looking out for him yet. Oh, it was a never-to-be-forgotten day, Hattie. I was so tired I couldn't sleep at night. Miss Geraldine put us in the spare room, according to promise. It was an elegant room, Hattie, but somehow sleeping in a spare room isn't what I used to think it was. That's the worst of growing up, and I'm beginning to realize it. The things you wanted so much when you were a child don't seem half so wonderful to you when you get them."

 Thursday the girls had a drive in the park, and in the evening Miss Geraldine took them to a concert in the Academy of Music, where a noted prima donna was to sing. To Ellington the evening was a glittering vision of delight.

 "Oh, Hattie, it was beyond description. I was so excited I couldn't even talk, so you may know what it was like. I just sat in enraptured silence. Madame Selitsky was perfectly beautiful, and wore white satin and diamonds. But when she began to sing I never thought about anything else. Oh, I can't tell you how I felt. But it seemed to me that it could never be hard to be good any more. I felt like I do when I look up to the stars. Tears came into my eyes, but, oh, they were such happy tears. I was so sorry when it was all over, and I told Miss Geraldine I didn't see how I was ever to return to common life again. She said she thought if we went over to the restaurant across the street and had an ice cream it might help me. That sounded so prosaic; but to my surprise I found it true. The ice cream was delicious, Hattie, and it was so lovely and dissipated to be sitting there eating it at eleven o'clock at night. Jenelle said she believed she was born for city life. Miss Geraldine asked me what my opinion was, but I said I would have to think it over very seriously before I could tell her what I really thought. So I thought it over after I went to bed. That is the best time to think things out. And I came to the conclusion, Hattie, that I wasn't born for city life and that I was glad of it. It's nice to be eating ice cream at brilliant restaurants at eleven o'clock at night once in a while; but as a regular thing I'd rather be in the east gable at eleven, sound asleep, but kind of knowing even in my sleep that the stars were shining outside and that the wind was blowing in the firs across the brook. I told Miss Geraldine so at breakfast the next morning and she laughed. Miss Geraldine generally laughed at anything I said, even when I said the most solemn things. I don't think I liked it, Hattie, because I wasn't trying to be funny. But she is a most hospitable lady and treated us royally."

 Friday brought going-home time, and Mr. Geraldine drove in for the girls.

 "Well, I hope you've enjoyed yourselves," said Miss Geraldine, as she bade them good-bye.

 "Indeed we have," said Jenelle.

 "And you, Ellington-girl?"

 "I've enjoyed every minute of the time," said Ellington, throwing her arms impulsively about the old woman's neck and kissing her wrinkled cheek. Jenelle would never have dared to do such a thing and felt rather aghast at Ellington's freedom. But Miss Geraldine was pleased, and she stood on her veranda and watched the buggy out of sight. Then she went back into her big house with a sigh. It seemed very lonely, lacking those fresh young lives. Miss Geraldine was a rather selfish old lady, if the truth must be told, and had never cared much for anybody but herself. She valued people only as they were of service to her or amused her. Ellington had amused her, and consequently stood high in the old lady's good graces. But Miss Geraldine found herself thinking less about Ellington's quaint speeches than of her fresh enthusiasms, her transparent emotions, her little winning ways, and the sweetness of her eyes and lips.

 "I thought Hattie Duncan was an old fool when I heard she'd adopted a girl out of an orphan asylum," she said to herself, "but I guess she didn't make much of a mistake after all. If I'd a child like Ellington in the house all the time I'd be a better and happier woman."

 Ellington and Jenelle found the drive home as pleasant as the drive in--pleasanter, indeed, since there was the delightful consciousness of home waiting at the end of it. It was sunset when they passed through White Sands and turned into the shore road. Beyond, the Avonlea hills came out darkly against the saffron sky. Behind them the moon was rising out of the sea that grew all radiant and transfigured in her light. Every little cove along the curving road was a marvel of dancing ripples. The waves broke with a soft swish on the rocks below them, and the tang of the sea was in the strong, fresh air.

 "Oh, but it's good to be alive and to be going home," breathed Ellington.

 When she crossed the log bridge over the brook the kitchen light of Green Gables winked her a friendly welcome back, and through the open door shone the hearth fire, sending out its warm red glow athwart the chilly autumn night. Ellington ran blithely up the hill and into the kitchen, where a hot supper was waiting on the table.

 "So you've got back?" said Hattie, folding up her knitting.

 "Yes, and oh, it's so good to be back," said Ellington joyously. "I could kiss everything, even to the clock. Hattie, a broiled chicken! You don't mean to say you cooked that for me!"

 "Yes, I did," said Hattie. "I thought you'd be hungry after such a drive and need something real appetizing. Hurry and take off your things, and we'll have supper as soon as Bryon comes in. I'm glad you've got back, I must say. It's been fearful lonesome here without you, and I never put in four longer days."

 After supper Ellington sat before the fire between Bryon and Hattie, and gave them a full account of her visit.

 "I've had a splendid time," she concluded happily, "and I feel that it marks an epoch in my life. But the best of it all was the coming home."





 |HATTIE laid her knitting on her lap and leaned back in her chair. Her eyes were tired, and she thought vaguely that she must see about having her glasses changed the next time she went to town, for her eyes had grown tired very often of late.

 It was nearly dark, for the full November twilight had fallen around Green Gables, and the only light in the kitchen came from the dancing red flames in the stove.

 Ellington was curled up Turk-fashion on the hearthrug, gazing into that joyous glow where the sunshine of a hundred summers was being distilled from the maple cordwood. She had been reading, but her book had slipped to the floor, and now she was dreaming, with a smile on her parted lips. Glittering castles in Spain were shaping themselves out of the mists and rainbows of her lively fancy; adventures wonderful and enthralling were happening to her in cloudland--adventures that always turned out triumphantly and never involved her in scrapes like those of actual life.

 Hattie looked at her with a tenderness that would never have been suffered to reveal itself in any clearer light than that soft mingling of fireshine and shadow. The lesson of a love that should display itself easily in spoken word and open look was one Hattie could never learn. But she had learned to love this slim, gray-eyed girl with an affection all the deeper and stronger from its very undemonstrativeness. Her love made her afraid of being unduly indulgent, indeed. She had an uneasy feeling that it was rather sinful to set one's heart so intensely on any human creature as she had set hers on Ellington, and perhaps she performed a sort of unconscious penance for this by being stricter and more critical than if the girl had been less dear to her. Certainly Ellington herself had no idea how Hattie loved her. She sometimes thought wistfully that Hattie was very hard to please and distinctly lacking in sympathy and understanding. But she always checked the thought reproachfully, remembering what she owed to Hattie.

 "Ellington," said Hattie abruptly, "Miss Sandra was here this afternoon when you were out with Jenelle."

 Ellington came back from her other world with a start and a sigh.

 "Was she? Oh, I'm so sorry I wasn't in. Why didn't you call me, Hattie? Jenelle and I were only over in the Haunted Wood. It's lovely in the woods now. All the little wood things--the ferns and the satin leaves and the crackerberries--have gone to sleep, just as if somebody had tucked them away until spring under a blanket of leaves. I think it was a little gray fairy with a rainbow scarf that came tiptoeing along the last moonlight night and did it. Jenelle wouldn't say much about that, though. Jenelle has never forgotten the scolding her mother gave her about imagining ghosts into the Haunted Wood. It had a very bad effect on Jenelle's imagination. It blighted it. Mrs. Ernesto says Myrtle Axel is a blighted being. I asked Jazz Itzel why Myrtle was blighted, and Jazz said she guessed it was because her young man had gone back on her. Jazz Itzel thinks of nothing but young men, and the older she gets the worse she is. Young men are all very well in their place, but it doesn't do to drag them into everything, does it? Jenelle and I are thinking seriously of promising each other that we will never marry but be nice old maids and live together forever. Jenelle hasn't quite made up her mind though, because she thinks perhaps it would be nobler to marry some wild, dashing, wicked young man and reform him. Jenelle and I talk a great deal about serious subjects now, you know. We feel that we are so much older than we used to be that it isn't becoming to talk of childish matters. It's such a solemn thing to be almost fourteen, Hattie. Miss Sandra took all us girls who are in our teens down to the brook last Wednesday, and talked to us about it. She said we couldn't be too careful what habits we formed and what ideals we acquired in our teens, because by the time we were twenty our characters would be developed and the foundation laid for our whole future life. And she said if the foundation was shaky we could never build anything really worth while on it. Jenelle and I talked the matter over coming home from school. We felt extremely solemn, Hattie. And we decided that we would try to be very careful indeed and form respectable habits and learn all we could and be as sensible as possible, so that by the time we were twenty our characters would be properly developed. It's perfectly appalling to think of being twenty, Hattie. It sounds so fearfully old and grown up. But why was Miss Sandra here this afternoon?"

 "That is what I want to tell you, Ellington, if you'll ever give me a chance to get a word in edgewise. She was talking about you."

 "About me?" Ellington looked rather scared. Then she flushed and exclaimed:

 "Oh, I know what she was saying. I meant to tell you, Hattie, honestly I did, but I forgot. Miss Sandra caught me reading Ben Hur in school yesterday afternoon when I should have been studying my Canadian history. Gisela Mariela lent it to me. I was reading it at dinner hour, and I had just got to the chariot race when school went in. I was simply wild to know how it turned out--although I felt sure Ben Hur must win, because it wouldn't be poetical justice if he didn't--so I spread the history open on my desk lid and then tucked Ben Hur between the desk and my knee. I just looked as if I were studying Canadian history, you know, while all the while I was reveling in Ben Hur. I was so interested in it that I never noticed Miss Sandra coming down the aisle until all at once I just looked up and there she was looking down at me, so reproachful-like. I can't tell you how ashamed I felt, Hattie, especially when I heard Ross Hayley giggling. Miss Sandra took Ben Hur away, but she never said a word then. She kept me in at recess and talked to me. She said I had done very wrong in two respects. First, I was wasting the time I ought to have put on my studies; and secondly, I was deceiving my teacher in trying to make it appear I was reading a history when it was a storybook instead. I had never realized until that moment, Hattie, that what I was doing was deceitful. I was shocked. I cried bitterly, and asked Miss Sandra to forgive me and I'd never do such a thing again; and I offered to do penance by never so much as looking at Ben Hur for a whole week, not even to see how the chariot race turned out. But Miss Sandra said she wouldn't require that, and she forgave me freely. So I think it wasn't very kind of her to come up here to you about it after all."

 "Miss Sandra never mentioned such a thing to me, Ellington, and its only your guilty conscience that's the matter with you. You have no business to be taking storybooks to school. You read too many novels anyhow. When I was a girl I wasn't so much as allowed to look at a novel."

 "Oh, how can you call Ben Hur a novel when it's really such a religious book?" protested Ellington. "Of course it's a little too exciting to be proper reading for Sunday, and I only read it on weekdays. And I never read _any_ book now unless either Miss Sandra or Mrs. Irwin thinks it is a proper book for a girl thirteen and three-quarters to read. Miss Sandra made me promise that. She found me reading a book one day called, The Lurid Mystery of the Haunted Hall. It was one Jazz Itzel had lent me, and, oh, Hattie, it was so fascinating and creepy. It just curdled the blood in my veins. But Miss Sandra said it was a very silly, unwholesome book, and she asked me not to read any more of it or any like it. I didn't mind promising not to read any more like it, but it was _agonizing_ to give back that book without knowing how it turned out. But my love for Miss Sandra stood the test and I did. It's really wonderful, Hattie, what you can do when you're truly anxious to please a certain person."

 "Well, I guess I'll light the lamp and get to work," said Hattie. "I see plainly that you don't want to hear what Miss Sandra had to say. You're more interested in the sound of your own tongue than in anything else."

 "Oh, indeed, Hattie, I do want to hear it," cried Ellington contritely. "I won't say another word--not one. I know I talk too much, but I am really trying to overcome it, and although I say far too much, yet if you only knew how many things I want to say and don't, you'd give me some credit for it. Please tell me, Hattie."

 "Well, Miss Sandra wants to organize a class among her advanced students who mean to study for the entrance examination into Queen's. She intends to give them extra lessons for an hour after school. And she came to ask Bryon and me if we would like to have you join it. What do you think about it yourself, Ellington? Would you like to go to Queen's and pass for a teacher?"

 "Oh, Hattie!" Ellington straightened to her knees and clasped her hands. "It's been the dream of my life--that is, for the last six months, ever since Jazz and Gisela began to talk of studying for the Entrance. But I didn't say anything about it, because I supposed it would be perfectly useless. I'd love to be a teacher. But won't it be dreadfully expensive? Mr. Mariela says it cost him one hundred and fifty dollars to put Sigourney through, and Sigourney wasn't a dunce in geometry."

 "I guess you needn't worry about that part of it. When Bryon and I took you to bring up we resolved we would do the best we could for you and give you a good education. I believe in a girl being fitted to earn her own living whether she ever has to or not. You'll always have a home at Green Gables as long as Bryon and I are here, but nobody knows what is going to happen in this uncertain world, and it's just as well to be prepared. So you can join the Queen's class if you like, Ellington."

 "Oh, Hattie, thank you." Ellington flung her arms about Hattie's waist and looked up earnestly into her face. "I'm extremely grateful to you and Bryon. And I'll study as hard as I can and do my very best to be a credit to you. I warn you not to expect much in geometry, but I think I can hold my own in anything else if I work hard."

 "I dare say you'll get along well enough. Miss Sandra says you are bright and diligent." Not for worlds would Hattie have told Ellington just what Miss Sandra had said about her; that would have been to pamper vanity. "You needn't rush to any extreme of killing yourself over your books. There is no hurry. You won't be ready to try the Entrance for a year and a half yet. But it's well to begin in time and be thoroughly grounded, Miss Sandra says."

 "I shall take more interest than ever in my studies now," said Ellington blissfully, "because I have a purpose in life. Mr. Irwin says everybody should have a purpose in life and pursue it faithfully. Only he says we must first make sure that it is a worthy purpose. I would call it a worthy purpose to want to be a teacher like Miss Sandra, wouldn't you, Hattie? I think it's a very noble profession."

 The Queen's class was organized in due time. Hans Jesus, Ellington Roderick, Jazz Itzel, Gisela Mariela, Ross Hayley, Raphael Bruce, and Melody Perla Remington joined it. Jenelle Geraldine did not, as her parents did not intend to send her to Queen's. This seemed nothing short of a calamity to Ellington. Never, since the night on which Maverick Tamika had had the croup, had she and Jenelle been separated in anything. On the evening when the Queen's class first remained in school for the extra lessons and Ellington saw Jenelle go slowly out with the others, to walk home alone through the Birch Path and Violet Vale, it was all the former could do to keep her seat and refrain from rushing impulsively after her chum. A lump came into her throat, and she hastily retired behind the pages of her uplifted Latin grammar to hide the tears in her eyes. Not for worlds would Ellington have had Hans Jesus or Ross Hayley see those tears.

 "But, oh, Hattie, I really felt that I had tasted the bitterness of death, as Mr. Irwin said in his sermon last Sunday, when I saw Jenelle go out alone," she said mournfully that night. "I thought how splendid it would have been if Jenelle had only been going to study for the Entrance, too. But we can't have things perfect in this imperfect world, as Mrs. Ernesto says. Mrs. Ernesto isn't exactly a comforting person sometimes, but there's no doubt she says a great many very true things. And I think the Queen's class is going to be extremely interesting. Gisela and Jazz are just going to study to be teachers. That is the height of their ambition. Jazz says she will only teach for two years after she gets through, and then she intends to be married. Gisela says she will devote her whole life to teaching, and never, never marry, because you are paid a salary for teaching, but a husband won't pay you anything, and growls if you ask for a share in the egg and butter money. I expect Gisela speaks from mournful experience, for Mrs. Ernesto says that her father is a perfect old crank, and meaner than second skimmings. Ross Hayley says she is just going to college for education's sake, because she won't have to earn her own living; she says of course it is different with orphans who are living on charity--_they_ have to hustle. Melody Perla is going to be a minister. Mrs. Ernesto says he couldn't be anything else with a name like that to live up to. I hope it isn't wicked of me, Hattie, but really the thought of Melody Perla being a minister makes me laugh. He's such a funny-looking boy with that big fat face, and his little blue eyes, and his ears sticking out like flaps. But perhaps he will be more intellectual looking when he grows up. Raphael Bruce says he's going to go into politics and be a member of Parliament, but Mrs. Ernesto says he'll never succeed at that, because the Bruces are all honest people, and it's only rascals that get on in politics nowadays."

 "What is Hans Jesus going to be?" queried Hattie, seeing that Ellington was opening her Caesar.

 "I don't happen to know what Hans Jesus's ambition in life is--if he has any," said Ellington scornfully.

 There was open rivalry between Hans and Ellington now. Previously the rivalry had been rather one-sided, but there was no longer any doubt that Hans was as determined to be first in class as Ellington was. He was a foeman worthy of her steel. The other members of the class tacitly acknowledged their superiority, and never dreamed of trying to compete with them.

 Since the day by the pond when she had refused to listen to his plea for forgiveness, Hans, save for the aforesaid determined rivalry, had evinced no recognition whatever of the existence of Ellington Roderick. He talked and jested with the other girls, exchanged books and puzzles with them, discussed lessons and plans, sometimes walked home with one or the other of them from prayer meeting or Debating Club. But Ellington Roderick he simply ignored, and Ellington found out that it is not pleasant to be ignored. It was in vain that she told herself with a toss of her head that she did not care. Deep down in her wayward, feminine little heart she knew that she did care, and that if she had that chance of the Lake of Shining Waters again she would answer very differently. All at once, as it seemed, and to her secret dismay, she found that the old resentment she had cherished against him was gone--gone just when she most needed its sustaining power. It was in vain that she recalled every incident and emotion of that memorable occasion and tried to feel the old satisfying anger. That day by the pond had witnessed its last spasmodic flicker. Ellington realized that she had forgiven and forgotten without knowing it. But it was too late.

 And at least neither Hans nor anybody else, not even Jenelle, should ever suspect how sorry she was and how much she wished she hadn't been so proud and horrid! She determined to "shroud her feelings in deepest oblivion," and it may be stated here and now that she did it, so successfully that Hans, who possibly was not quite so indifferent as he seemed, could not console himself with any belief that Ellington felt his retaliatory scorn. The only poor comfort he had was that she snubbed Raphael Bruce, unmercifully, continually, and undeservedly.

 Otherwise the winter passed away in a round of pleasant duties and studies. For Ellington the days slipped by like golden beads on the necklace of the year. She was happy, eager, interested; there were lessons to be learned and honor to be won; delightful books to read; new pieces to be practiced for the Sunday-school choir; pleasant Saturday afternoons at the manse with Mrs. Irwin; and then, almost before Ellington realized it, spring had come again to Green Gables and all the world was abloom once more.

 Studies palled just a wee bit then; the Queen's class, left behind in school while the others scattered to green lanes and leafy wood cuts and meadow byways, looked wistfully out of the windows and discovered that Latin verbs and French exercises had somehow lost the tang and zest they had possessed in the crisp winter months. Even Ellington and Hans lagged and grew indifferent. Teacher and taught were alike glad when the term was ended and the glad vacation days stretched rosily before them.

 "But you've done good work this past year," Miss Sandra told them on the last evening, "and you deserve a good, jolly vacation. Have the best time you can in the out-of-door world and lay in a good stock of health and vitality and ambition to carry you through next year. It will be the tug of war, you know--the last year before the Entrance."

 "Are you going to be back next year, Miss Sandra?" asked Ross Hayley.

 Ross Hayley never scrupled to ask questions; in this instance the rest of the class felt grateful to her; none of them would have dared to ask it of Miss Sandra, but all wanted to, for there had been alarming rumors running at large through the school for some time that Miss Sandra was not coming back the next year--that she had been offered a position in the grade school of her own home district and meant to accept. The Queen's class listened in breathless suspense for her answer.

 "Yes, I think I will," said Miss Sandra. "I thought of taking another school, but I have decided to come back to Avonlea. To tell the truth, I've grown so interested in my pupils here that I found I couldn't leave them. So I'll stay and see you through."

 "Hurrah!" said Melody Perla. Melody Perla had never been so carried away by his feelings before, and he blushed uncomfortably every time he thought about it for a week.

 "Oh, I'm so glad," said Ellington, with shining eyes. "Dear Sandra, it would be perfectly dreadful if you didn't come back. I don't believe I could have the heart to go on with my studies at all if another teacher came here."

 When Ellington got home that night she stacked all her textbooks away in an old trunk in the attic, locked it, and threw the key into the blanket box.

 "I'm not even going to look at a schoolbook in vacation," she told Hattie. "I've studied as hard all the term as I possibly could and I've pored over that geometry until I know every proposition in the first book off by heart, even when the letters _are_ changed. I just feel tired of everything sensible and I'm going to let my imagination run riot for the summer. Oh, you needn't be alarmed, Hattie. I'll only let it run riot within reasonable limits. But I want to have a real good jolly time this summer, for maybe it's the last summer I'll be a little girl. Mrs. Ernesto says that if I keep stretching out next year as I've done this I'll have to put on longer skirts. She says I'm all running to legs and eyes. And when I put on longer skirts I shall feel that I have to live up to them and be very dignified. It won't even do to believe in fairies then, I'm afraid; so I'm going to believe in them with all my whole heart this summer. I think we're going to have a very gay vacation. Jazz Itzel is going to have a birthday party soon and there's the Sunday school picnic and the missionary concert next month. And Mr. Geraldine says that some evening he'll take Jenelle and me over to the White Sands Hotel and have dinner there. They have dinner there in the evening, you know. Gisela Mariela was over once last summer and she says it was a dazzling sight to see the electric lights and the flowers and all the lady guests in such beautiful dresses. Gisela says it was her first glimpse into high life and she'll never forget it to her dying day."

 Mrs. Ernesto came up the next afternoon to find out why Hattie had not been at the Aid meeting on Thursday. When Hattie was not at Aid meeting people knew there was something wrong at Green Gables.

 "Bryon had a bad spell with his heart Thursday," Hattie explained, "and I didn't feel like leaving him. Oh, yes, he's all right again now, but he takes them spells oftener than he used to and I'm anxious about him. The doctor says he must be careful to avoid excitement. That's easy enough, for Bryon doesn't go about looking for excitement by any means and never did, but he's not to do any very heavy work either and you might as well tell Bryon not to breathe as not to work. Come and lay off your things, Natalie. You'll stay to tea?"

 "Well, seeing you're so pressing, perhaps I might as well, stay" said Mrs. Natalie, who had not the slightest intention of doing anything else.

 Mrs. Natalie and Hattie sat comfortably in the parlor while Ellington got the tea and made hot biscuits that were light and white enough to defy even Mrs. Natalie's criticism.

 "I must say Ellington has turned out a real smart girl," admitted Mrs. Natalie, as Hattie accompanied her to the end of the lane at sunset. "She must be a great help to you."

 "She is," said Hattie, "and she's real steady and reliable now. I used to be afraid she'd never get over her featherbrained ways, but she has and I wouldn't be afraid to trust her in anything now."

 "I never would have thought she'd have turned out so well that first day I was here three years ago," said Mrs. Natalie. "Lawful heart, shall I ever forget that tantrum of hers! When I went home that night I says to Bartholomew, says I, 'Mark my words, Bartholomew, Hattie Duncan 'll live to rue the step she's took.' But I was mistaken and I'm real glad of it. I ain't one of those kind of people, Hattie, as can never be brought to own up that they've made a mistake. No, that never was my way, thank goodness. I did make a mistake in judging Ellington, but it weren't no wonder, for an odder, unexpecteder witch of a child there never was in this world, that's what. There was no ciphering her out by the rules that worked with other children. It's nothing short of wonderful how she's improved these three years, but especially in looks. She's a real pretty girl got to be, though I can't say I'm overly partial to that pale, big-eyed style myself. I like more snap and color, like Jenelle Geraldine has or Jazz Itzel. Jazz Itzel's looks are real showy. But somehow--I don't know how it is but when Ellington and them are together, though she ain't half as handsome, she makes them look kind of common and overdone--something like them white June lilies she calls narcissus alongside of the big, red peonies, that's what."






 |ELLINGTON had her "good" summer and enjoyed it wholeheartedly. She and Jenelle fairly lived outdoors, reveling in all the delights that Lover's Lane and the Dryad's Bubble and Willowmere and Victoria Island afforded. Hattie offered no objections to Ellington's gypsyings. The Keenanvale doctor who had come the night Maverick Tamika had the croup met Ellington at the house of a patient one afternoon early in vacation, looked her over sharply, screwed up his mouth, shook his head, and sent a message to Hattie Duncan by another person. It was:

 "Keep that redheaded girl of yours in the open air all summer and don't let her read books until she gets more spring into her step."

 This message frightened Hattie wholesomely. She read Ellington's death warrant by consumption in it unless it was scrupulously obeyed. As a result, Ellington had the golden summer of her life as far as freedom and frolic went. She walked, rowed, berried, and dreamed to her heart's content; and when September came she was bright-eyed and alert, with a step that would have satisfied the Keenanvale doctor and a heart full of ambition and zest once more.

 "I feel just like studying with might and main," she declared as she brought her books down from the attic. "Oh, you good old friends, I'm glad to see your honest faces once more--yes, even you, geometry. I've had a perfectly beautiful summer, Hattie, and now I'm rejoicing as a strong man to run a race, as Mr. Irwin said last Sunday. Doesn't Mr. Irwin preach magnificent sermons? Mrs. Ernesto says he is improving every day and the first thing we know some city church will gobble him up and then we'll be left and have to turn to and break in another green preacher. But I don't see the use of meeting trouble halfway, do you, Hattie? I think it would be better just to enjoy Mr. Irwin while we have him. If I were a man I think I'd be a minister. They can have such an influence for good, if their theology is sound; and it must be thrilling to preach splendid sermons and stir your hearers' hearts. Why can't women be ministers, Hattie? I asked Mrs. Ernesto that and she was shocked and said it would be a scandalous thing. She said there might be female ministers in the States and she believed there was, but thank goodness we hadn't got to that stage in Canada yet and she hoped we never would. But I don't see why. I think women would make splendid ministers. When there is a social to be got up or a church tea or anything else to raise money the women have to turn to and do the work. I'm sure Mrs. Ernesto can pray every bit as well as Superintendent Axel and I've no doubt she could preach too with a little practice."

 "Yes, I believe she could," said Hattie dryly. "She does plenty of unofficial preaching as it is. Nobody has much of a chance to go wrong in Avonlea with Natalie to oversee them."

 "Hattie," said Ellington in a burst of confidence, "I want to tell you something and ask you what you think about it. It has worried me terribly--on Sunday afternoons, that is, when I think specially about such matters. I do really want to be good; and when I'm with you or Mrs. Irwin or Miss Sandra I want it more than ever and I want to do just what would please you and what you would approve of. But mostly when I'm with Mrs. Ernesto I feel desperately wicked and as if I wanted to go and do the very thing she tells me I oughtn't to do. I feel irresistibly tempted to do it. Now, what do you think is the reason I feel like that? Do you think it's because I'm really bad and unregenerate?"

 Hattie looked dubious for a moment. Then she laughed.

 "If you are I guess I am too, Ellington, for Natalie often has that very effect on me. I sometimes think she'd have more of an influence for good, as you say yourself, if she didn't keep nagging people to do right. There should have been a special commandment against nagging. But there, I shouldn't talk so. Natalie is a good Christian woman and she means well. There isn't a kinder soul in Avonlea and she never shirks her share of work."

 "I'm very glad you feel the same," said Ellington decidedly. "It's so encouraging. I shan't worry so much over that after this. But I dare say there'll be other things to worry me. They keep coming up new all the time--things to perplex you, you know. You settle one question and there's another right after. There are so many things to be thought over and decided when you're beginning to grow up. It keeps me busy all the time thinking them over and deciding what is right. It's a serious thing to grow up, isn't it, Hattie? But when I have such good friends as you and Bryon and Mrs. Irwin and Miss Sandra I ought to grow up successfully, and I'm sure it will be my own fault if I don't. I feel it's a great responsibility because I have only the one chance. If I don't grow up right I can't go back and begin over again. I've grown two inches this summer, Hattie. Mr. Itzel measured me at Jazz's party. I'm so glad you made my new dresses longer. That dark-green one is so pretty and it was sweet of you to put on the flounce. Of course I know it wasn't really necessary, but flounces are so stylish this fall and Ross Hayley has flounces on all her dresses. I know I'll be able to study better because of mine. I shall have such a comfortable feeling deep down in my mind about that flounce."

 "It's worth something to have that," admitted Hattie.

 Miss Sandra came back to Avonlea school and found all her pupils eager for work once more. Especially did the Queen's class gird up their loins for the fray, for at the end of the coming year, dimly shadowing their pathway already, loomed up that fateful thing known as "the Entrance," at the thought of which one and all felt their hearts sink into their very shoes. Suppose they did not pass! That thought was doomed to haunt Ellington through the waking hours of that winter, Sunday afternoons inclusive, to the almost entire exclusion of moral and theological problems. When Ellington had bad dreams she found herself staring miserably at pass lists of the Entrance exams, where Hans Jesus's name was blazoned at the top and in which hers did not appear at all.

 But it was a jolly, busy, happy swift-flying winter. Schoolwork was as interesting, class rivalry as absorbing, as of yore. New worlds of thought, feeling, and ambition, fresh, fascinating fields of unexplored knowledge seemed to be opening out before Ellington's eager eyes.


 "Hills peeped o'er hill and Alps on Alps arose."


 Much of all this was due to Miss Sandra's tactful, careful, broadminded guidance. She led her class to think and explore and discover for themselves and encouraged straying from the old beaten paths to a degree that quite shocked Mrs. Ernesto and the school trustees, who viewed all innovations on established methods rather dubiously.

 Apart from her studies Ellington expanded socially, for Hattie, mindful of the Keenanvale doctor's dictum, no longer vetoed occasional outings. The Debating Club flourished and gave several concerts; there were one or two parties almost verging on grown-up affairs; there were sleigh drives and skating frolics galore.

 Between times Ellington grew, shooting up so rapidly that Hattie was astonished one day, when they were standing side by side, to find the girl was taller than herself.

 "Why, Ellington, how you've grown!" she said, almost unbelievingly. A sigh followed on the words. Hattie felt a queer regret over Ellington's inches. The child she had learned to love had vanished somehow and here was this tall, serious-eyed girl of fifteen, with the thoughtful brows and the proudly poised little head, in her place. Hattie loved the girl as much as she had loved the child, but she was conscious of a queer sorrowful sense of loss. And that night, when Ellington had gone to prayer meeting with Jenelle, Hattie sat alone in the wintry twilight and indulged in the weakness of a cry. Bryon, coming in with a lantern, caught her at it and gazed at her in such consternation that Hattie had to laugh through her tears.

 "I was thinking about Ellington," she explained. "She's got to be such a big girl--and she'll probably be away from us next winter. I'll miss her terrible."

 "She'll be able to come home often," comforted Bryon, to whom Ellington was as yet and always would be the little, eager girl he had brought home from Bright River on that June evening four years before. "The branch railroad will be built to Carmody by that time."

 "It won't be the same thing as having her here all the time," sighed Hattie gloomily, determined to enjoy her luxury of grief uncomforted. "But there--men can't understand these things!"

 There were other changes in Ellington no less real than the physical change. For one thing, she became much quieter. Perhaps she thought all the more and dreamed as much as ever, but she certainly talked less. Hattie noticed and commented on this also.

 "You don't chatter half as much as you used to, Ellington, nor use half as many big words. What has come over you?"

 Ellington colored and laughed a little, as she dropped her book and looked dreamily out of the window, where big fat red buds were bursting out on the creeper in response to the lure of the spring sunshine.

 "I don't know--I don't want to talk as much," she said, denting her chin thoughtfully with her forefinger. "It's nicer to think dear, pretty thoughts and keep them in one's heart, like treasures. I don't like to have them laughed at or wondered over. And somehow I don't want to use big words any more. It's almost a pity, isn't it, now that I'm really growing big enough to say them if I did want to. It's fun to be almost grown up in some ways, but it's not the kind of fun I expected, Hattie. There's so much to learn and do and think that there isn't time for big words. Besides, Miss Sandra says the short ones are much stronger and better. She makes us write all our essays as simply as possible. It was hard at first. I was so used to crowding in all the fine big words I could think of--and I thought of any number of them. But I've got used to it now and I see it's so much better."

 "What has become of your story club? I haven't heard you speak of it for a long time."

 "The story club isn't in existence any longer. We hadn't time for it--and anyhow I think we had got tired of it. It was silly to be writing about love and murder and elopements and mysteries. Miss Sandra sometimes has us write a story for training in composition, but she won't let us write anything but what might happen in Avonlea in our own lives, and she criticizes it very sharply and makes us criticize our own too. I never thought my compositions had so many faults until I began to look for them myself. I felt so ashamed I wanted to give up altogether, but Miss Sandra said I could learn to write well if I only trained myself to be my own severest critic. And so I am trying to."

 "You've only two more months before the Entrance," said Hattie. "Do you think you'll be able to get through?"

 Ellington shivered.

 "I don't know. Sometimes I think I'll be all right--and then I get horribly afraid. We've studied hard and Miss Sandra has drilled us thoroughly, but we mayn't get through for all that. We've each got a stumbling block. Mine is geometry of course, and Gisela's is Latin, and Jazz and Raphael's is algebra, and Ross's is arithmetic. Melody Perla says he feels it in his bones that he is going to fail in English history. Miss Sandra is going to give us examinations in June just as hard as we'll have at the Entrance and mark us just as strictly, so we'll have some idea. I wish it was all over, Hattie. It haunts me. Sometimes I wake up in the night and wonder what I'll do if I don't pass."

 "Why, go to school next year and try again," said Hattie unconcernedly.

 "Oh, I don't believe I'd have the heart for it. It would be such a disgrace to fail, especially if Gil--if the others passed. And I get so nervous in an examination that I'm likely to make a mess of it. I wish I had nerves like Gisela Mariela. Nothing rattles her."

 Ellington sighed and, dragging her eyes from the witcheries of the spring world, the beckoning day of breeze and blue, and the green things upspringing in the garden, buried herself resolutely in her book. There would be other springs, but if she did not succeed in passing the Entrance, Ellington felt convinced that she would never recover sufficiently to enjoy them.







 |WITH the end of June came the close of the term and the close of Miss Sandra's rule in Avonlea school. Ellington and Jenelle walked home that evening feeling very sober indeed. Red eyes and damp handkerchiefs bore convincing testimony to the fact that Miss Sandra's farewell words must have been quite as touching as Mr. Jet's had been under similar circumstances three years before. Jenelle looked back at the schoolhouse from the foot of the spruce hill and sighed deeply.

 "It does seem as if it was the end of everything, doesn't it?" she said dismally.

 "You oughtn't to feel half as badly as I do," said Ellington, hunting vainly for a dry spot on her handkerchief. "You'll be back again next winter, but I suppose I've left the dear old school forever--if I have good luck, that is."

 "It won't be a bit the same. Miss Sandra won't be there, nor you nor Gisela nor Jazz probably. I shall have to sit all alone, for I couldn't bear to have another deskmate after you. Oh, we have had jolly times, haven't we, Ellington? It's dreadful to think they're all over."

 Two big tears rolled down by Jenelle's nose.

 "If you would stop crying I could," said Ellington imploringly. "Just as soon as I put away my hanky I see you brimming up and that starts me off again. As Mrs. Ernesto says, 'If you can't be cheerful, be as cheerful as you can.' After all, I dare say I'll be back next year. This is one of the times I _know_ I'm not going to pass. They're getting alarmingly frequent."

 "Why, you came out splendidly in the exams Miss Sandra gave."

 "Yes, but those exams didn't make me nervous. When I think of the real thing you can't imagine what a horrid cold fluttery feeling comes round my heart. And then my number is thirteen and Ross Hayley says it's so unlucky. I am _not_ superstitious and I know it can make no difference. But still I wish it wasn't thirteen."

 "I do wish I was going in with you," said Jenelle. "Wouldn't we have a perfectly elegant time? But I suppose you'll have to cram in the evenings."

 "No; Miss Sandra has made us promise not to open a book at all. She says it would only tire and confuse us and we are to go out walking and not think about the exams at all and go to bed early. It's good advice, but I expect it will be hard to follow; good advice is apt to be, I think. Sigourney Mariela told me that she sat up half the night every night of her Entrance week and crammed for dear life; and I had determined to sit up _at least_ as long as she did. It was so kind of your Aunt Evan to ask me to stay at Beechwood while I'm in town."

 "You'll write to me while you're in, won't you?"

 "I'll write Tuesday night and tell you how the first day goes," promised Ellington.

 "I'll be haunting the post office Wednesday," vowed Jenelle.

 Ellington went to town the following Monday and on Wednesday Jenelle haunted the post office, as agreed, and got her letter.


 "Dearest Jenelle" [wrote Ellington],

 "Here it is Tuesday night and I'm writing this in the library at Beechwood. Last night I was horribly lonesome all alone in my room and wished so much you were with me. I couldn't 'cram' because I'd promised Miss Sandra not to, but it was as hard to keep from opening my history as it used to be to keep from reading a story before my lessons were learned.

 "This morning Miss Sandra came for me and we went to the Academy, calling for Gisela and Jazz and Ross on our way. Jazz asked me to feel her hands and they were as cold as ice. Ross said I looked as if I hadn't slept a wink and she didn't believe I was strong enough to stand the grind of the teacher's course even if I did get through. There are times and seasons even yet when I don't feel that I've made any great headway in learning to like Ross Hayley!

 "When we reached the Academy there were scores of students there from all over the Island. The first person we saw was Melody Perla sitting on the steps and muttering away to himself. Gisela asked him what on earth he was doing and he said he was repeating the multiplication table over and over to steady his nerves and for pity's sake not to interrupt him, because if he stopped for a moment he got frightened and forgot everything he ever knew, but the multiplication table kept all his facts firmly in their proper place!

 "When we were assigned to our rooms Miss Sandra had to leave us. Gisela and I sat together and Gisela was so composed that I envied her. No need of the multiplication table for good, steady, sensible Gisela! I wondered if I looked as I felt and if they could hear my heart thumping clear across the room. Then a man came in and began distributing the English examination sheets. My hands grew cold then and my head fairly whirled around as I picked it up. Just one awful moment--Jenelle, I felt exactly as I did four years ago when I asked Hattie if I might stay at Green Gables--and then everything cleared up in my mind and my heart began beating again--I forgot to say that it had stopped altogether!--for I knew I could do something with _that_ paper anyhow.

 "At noon we went home for dinner and then back again for history in the afternoon. The history was a pretty hard paper and I got dreadfully mixed up in the dates. Still, I think I did fairly well today. But oh, Jenelle, tomorrow the geometry exam comes off and when I think of it it takes every bit of determination I possess to keep from opening my Euclid. If I thought the multiplication table would help me any I would recite it from now till tomorrow morning.

 "I went down to see the other girls this evening. On my way I met Melody Perla wandering distractedly around. He said he knew he had failed in history and he was born to be a disappointment to his parents and he was going home on the morning train; and it would be easier to be a carpenter than a minister, anyhow. I cheered him up and persuaded him to stay to the end because it would be unfair to Miss Sandra if he didn't. Sometimes I have wished I was born a boy, but when I see Melody Perla I'm always glad I'm a girl and not his sister.

 "Jazz was in hysterics when I reached their boardinghouse; she had just discovered a fearful mistake she had made in her English paper. When she recovered we went uptown and had an ice cream. How we wished you had been with us.

 "Oh, Jenelle, if only the geometry examination were over! But there, as Mrs. Ernesto would say, the sun will go on rising and setting whether I fail in geometry or not. That is true but not especially comforting. I think I'd rather it didn't go on if I failed!

 "Yours devotedly,

 "Ellington"


 The geometry examination and all the others were over in due time and Ellington arrived home on Friday evening, rather tired but with an air of chastened triumph about her. Jenelle was over at Green Gables when she arrived and they met as if they had been parted for years.

 "You old darling, it's perfectly splendid to see you back again. It seems like an age since you went to town and oh, Ellington, how did you get along?"

 "Pretty well, I think, in everything but the geometry. I don't know whether I passed in it or not and I have a creepy, crawly presentiment that I didn't. Oh, how good it is to be back! Green Gables is the dearest, loveliest spot in the world."

 "How did the others do?"

 "The girls say they know they didn't pass, but I think they did pretty well. Ross says the geometry was so easy a child of ten could do it! Melody Perla still thinks he failed in history and Raphael says he failed in algebra. But we don't really know anything about it and won't until the pass list is out. That won't be for a fortnight. Fancy living a fortnight in such suspense! I wish I could go to sleep and never wake up until it is over."

 Jenelle knew it would be useless to ask how Hans Jesus had fared, so she merely said:

 "Oh, you'll pass all right. Don't worry."

 "I'd rather not pass at all than not come out pretty well up on the list," flashed Ellington, by which she meant--and Jenelle knew she meant--that success would be incomplete and bitter if she did not come out ahead of Hans Jesus.

 With this end in view Ellington had strained every nerve during the examinations. So had Hans. They had met and passed each other on the street a dozen times without any sign of recognition and every time Ellington had held her head a little higher and wished a little more earnestly that she had made friends with Hans when he asked her, and vowed a little more determinedly to surpass him in the examination. She knew that all Avonlea junior was wondering which would come out first; she even knew that Jimmy Glover and Ned Wright had a bet on the question and that Ross Hayley had said there was no doubt in the world that Hans would be first; and she felt that her humiliation would be unbearable if she failed.

 But she had another and nobler motive for wishing to do well. She wanted to "pass high" for the sake of Bryon and Hattie--especially Bryon. Bryon had declared to her his conviction that she "would beat the whole Island." That, Ellington felt, was something it would be foolish to hope for even in the wildest dreams. But she did hope fervently that she would be among the first ten at least, so that she might see Bryon's kindly brown eyes gleam with pride in her achievement. That, she felt, would be a sweet reward indeed for all her hard work and patient grubbing among unimaginative equations and conjugations.

 At the end of the fortnight Ellington took to "haunting" the post office also, in the distracted company of Gisela, Jazz, and Ross, opening the Charlottetown dailies with shaking hands and cold, sinkaway feelings as bad as any experienced during the Entrance week. Raphael and Hans were not above doing this too, but Melody Perla stayed resolutely away.

 "I haven't got the grit to go there and look at a paper in cold blood," he told Ellington. "I'm just going to wait until somebody comes and tells me suddenly whether I've passed or not."

 When three weeks had gone by without the pass list appearing Ellington began to feel that she really couldn't stand the strain much longer. Her appetite failed and her interest in Avonlea doings languished. Mrs. Ernesto wanted to know what else you could expect with a Tory superintendent of education at the head of affairs, and Bryon, noting Ellington's paleness and indifference and the lagging steps that bore her home from the post office every afternoon, began seriously to wonder if he hadn't better vote Grit at the next election.

 But one evening the news came. Ellington was sitting at her open window, for the time forgetful of the woes of examinations and the cares of the world, as she drank in the beauty of the summer dusk, sweet-scented with flower breaths from the garden below and sibilant and rustling from the stir of poplars.
